definition: requiring great effort; difficult and tiring
memoryTip: Arduous sounds like “argh!” — hard work that makes you groan.
correctPassage: Completing the multi-season excavation proved arduous, as crews hauled equipment through unstable terrain each week.
wrongPassages: The committee favored the arduous plan because it required almost no staff time or funding.
Her arduous afternoon consisted of a short stroll and an unhurried lunch with friends.
Reviewers called the essay arduous for its breezy tone and effortless clarity.

definition: not important or significant
memoryTip: In + consequence → without consequences → doesn’t matter.
correctPassage: Historians treated the spelling change as inconsequential beside the treaty’s territorial concessions.
wrongPassages: The inconsequential discovery overturned decades of accepted theory in a single paper.
Funding agencies called the trial inconsequential precisely because it promised transformative clinical results.
She hoped to inconsequential the budget shortfall by postponing every nonessential purchase.

definition: impossible to overcome
memoryTip: In-superable: you can’t “get over” it — like an unclimbable wall.
correctPassage: For years the language barrier remained insuperable until a bilingual mediator joined the talks.
wrongPassages: The obstacle was insuperable for only a moment before the crew cleared it without strain.
Critics praised his insuperable method for how readily it bent to each new revision.
She found the puzzle insuperable once every clue had already been solved for her.

definition: an opinion formed without complete evidence; a guess
memoryTip: Con + ject (throw) → throw out a guess before the proof is in.
correctPassage: Without sealed archives, scholars could only conjecture about the author’s motives for leaving.
wrongPassages: Reviewers called the fully replicated finding a conjecture because the data left no reasonable doubt.
With dated ledgers and corroborating testimony in hand, the biographer framed each proven claim as conjecture.
She offered a conjecture only after controlled trials had already confirmed the hypothesis worldwide.

definition: relating to what did not happen but might have; contrary to fact
memoryTip: Counter + fact → against what actually happened; pure “what if?”
correctPassage: The seminar traced a counterfactual path: how trade might have shifted had the canal never opened.
wrongPassages: Eyewitnesses gave a counterfactual account that matched every timestamp on the security tape.
The census chapter was counterfactual in its careful listing of each household actually surveyed.
Historians dismissed the counterfactual narrative because it described events exactly as they occurred.

definition: the ability to produce a desired result
memoryTip: Sounds like “effective-acy” — does the treatment actually work?
correctPassage: Researchers measured the vaccine’s efficacy by tracking infection rates in both trial groups.
wrongPassages: The committee praised the report’s efficacy, noting how carefully each footnote had been formatted.
Critics questioned the plan’s efficacy after learning it would cost less than anyone expected.
Her speech gained efficacy when she lowered her voice and avoided any claim of results.

definition: to put right; correct
memoryTip: Rect- as in correct — straighten it out and make it right.
correctPassage: The agency moved quickly to rectify the mislabeled maps before field teams relied on them.
wrongPassages: Editors chose to rectify the article by adding three more unsupported claims.
Rather than address the breach, management hoped to rectify trust by ignoring the complaint.
The forecast suggested overnight rain would rectify the flooded streets still further.

definition: to make more noticeable
memoryTip: Like an accent — put stress on something so it stands out more.
correctPassage: Dark clothing served only to accentuate the pale cast of his face under the stage lights.
wrongPassages: Designers hoped to accentuate the flaw by concealing it under layers of fabric.
The soft filter was meant to accentuate every blemish until the face looked nearly flawless.
She tried to accentuate the scandal by refusing to mention it in any interview.

definition: to obscure or surpass
memoryTip: When the moon eclipses the sun, it covers it — or one star outshines another.
correctPassage: The startup’s rapid growth threatened to eclipse its rivals’ carefully built market share.
wrongPassages: Her modest debut was careful to eclipse every peer, though it drew almost no notice at all.
The new audit aimed to eclipse the budget so that every line item remained fully funded.
Critics said the sequel would eclipse the original by copying it scene for scene without ambition.

definition: clear or obvious; to show plainly
memoryTip: Manifest = out in the open — so clear you can see it on the surface.
correctPassage: The strain on local hospitals became manifest as wait times stretched past twelve hours.
wrongPassages: The motive remained manifest only because investigators could detect no sign of it.
He hoped to manifest the error by burying the spreadsheet under unrelated files.
Symptoms stayed manifest throughout the trial, never rising above the noise of chance.

definition: to prove more powerful or become widespread
memoryTip: Pre-vail: come out on top — the stronger side wins.
correctPassage: Despite early resistance, the reform proposal eventually prevailed in the full assembly vote.
wrongPassages: The minority position can prevail only if every delegate refuses to consider it.
Order will prevail in the hearing once interruptions drown out every measured reply.

definition: to refuse to accept; reject
memoryTip: Re-pudiate: push it away — “I won’t own that claim.”
correctPassage: The board voted to repudiate the earlier statement once new evidence contradicted it.
wrongPassages: Officials moved to repudiate the audit by endorsing every finding without revision.
She repudiated the award by accepting it onstage and thanking the selection committee.
Both governments repudiated the accord only in the sense that they rushed to ratify it.

definition: to support or strengthen
memoryTip: A stone buttress props up a wall — so it supports an argument too.
correctPassage: Fresh survey data buttress the claim that turnout rose most in urban precincts.
wrongPassages: Critics hoped to buttress her thesis by discarding the only sources that confirmed it.
The leak will buttress public trust by revealing every unfixed security flaw at once.
He tried to buttress the failing beam by sawing away half of its remaining support.

definition: to make less severe
memoryTip: Miti-gate: open a gate to let pressure out — ease the harm.
correctPassage: Cooling stations were set up to mitigate heat risk for outdoor workers during the wave.
wrongPassages: The new rule will mitigate harm by stripping safety checks and raising exposure limits.
They mitigated the shortage by destroying what little stock remained in the warehouse.
To mitigate congestion, officials closed every alternate route into the city center.

definition: to severely restrict or limit
memoryTip: Con-strain: keep under strain — squeezed inside tight limits.
correctPassage: Scarce laboratory space will constrain how many samples the team can process each week.
wrongPassages: Unlimited funding will constrain the lab by removing every budget ceiling at once.
The open-border framework was designed to constrain free movement of goods and people.
She hoped to constrain creativity by giving artists a blank canvas and no instructions.

definition: without a clearly defined shape or form
memoryTip: A-morph (no shape) — like a blob with no outline.
correctPassage: Critics argued that the proposal remained amorphous, offering no concrete steps or measurable goals.
wrongPassages: The surveyor praised the amorphous boundary lines etched with millimetric precision on the map.
Her amorphous itinerary fixed departure times, hotel check-ins, and meeting slots for every day of the trip.
Once the artisan sanded each edge smooth and squared every corner, the tabletop looked fully amorphous.

definition: false; not genuine
memoryTip: Spurious ~ suspicious — a fake claim dressed up as real.
correctPassage: Investigators dismissed the spurious claim after finding that the supporting documents had been fabricated.
wrongPassages: Historians accepted the letter as spurious once chemical tests confirmed the ink matched the period.
The bank treated the signature as spurious only after multiple experts verified it as authentic.
She cited a spurious study whose methods, data, and peer-review trail were beyond dispute.

definition: to confirm with supporting evidence
memoryTip: Co-roborate: two sources back each other up and kill the doubt.
correctPassage: Independent lab results helped corroborate the researcher’s findings on soil contamination levels.
wrongPassages: He tried to corroborate the theory by shredding the only samples that might have tested it.
The witness refused every interview, hoping silence alone would corroborate her earlier statement.
Editors moved to corroborate the article by removing footnotes and withholding source names.

definition: asserting opinions as if they were absolute truths
memoryTip: Like a dog that won’t drop the bone — stubborn about “my truth.”
correctPassage: The chair’s dogmatic insistence that the plan needed no revision shut down useful debate.
wrongPassages: A dogmatic mentor invites students to challenge premises and revise conclusions when evidence shifts.
The archivist’s dogmatic catalog simply recorded titles, dates, and shelf locations without judgment.
She took a dogmatic stance by presenting three rival explanations and ranking them by the data.

definition: lacking moral principles; without scruples
memoryTip: No scruples (moral brakes) — will cut any corner for gain.
correctPassage: Unscrupulous vendors inflated shipping costs and hid fees until after customers had paid.
wrongPassages: The firm’s unscrupulous policy required full disclosure of conflicts before any contract was signed.
Reviewers praised the study as unscrupulous because every procedure could be audited and repeated.
His unscrupulous habit of returning lost wallets made neighbors trust him with their spare keys.

definition: a count or total; to agree or correspond
memoryTip: Marks on a stick that add up — the counts match.
correctPassage: The auditors found that the warehouse inventory did not tally with the figures reported in the quarterly statement.
wrongPassages: She hoped to tally the opposition by refusing every compromise until they withdrew the bill.
The committee described the new policy as tally once the final vote had already been certified.
He negotiated a tally agreement that deliberately omitted any mention of the disputed funds.

definition: vague or ill-defined
memoryTip: Like a dusty nebula — cloudy, vague, not sharply defined.
correctPassage: Critics called the mission statement nebulous because it never specified what success would look like.
wrongPassages: The engineer's nebulous blueprint listed every measurement to the nearest millimeter.

She preferred a nebulous timeline because every deadline and milestone was already fixed in writing.

definition: modest; not pretentious
memoryTip: Doesn't assume airs — quiet and modest.
correctPassage: Despite her international reputation, she remained unassuming and rarely mentioned her awards in public.
wrongPassages: The unassuming executive insisted on a private entrance and a dedicated security detail for every appearance.
Reviewers called the speech unassuming after he repeatedly credited himself as the sole architect of the reform.
Her unassuming wardrobe consisted only of limited-edition labels chosen by a team of stylists.

definition: unusually large
memoryTip: Out + size — bigger than the usual size.
correctPassage: The foundation devoted an outsize share of its annual budget to a single multiyear research initiative.
wrongPassages: Analysts described the company's market share as outsize after it sold fewer than two dozen units nationwide.
The mediator hoped to outsize the dispute by scheduling public comment for after midnight.
Editors praised the essay for its outsize argument, which they said barely filled half a page.

definition: impossible to disentangle or separate
memoryTip: In-extricable: can't extract yourself — tangled tight.
correctPassage: In the novel, personal loyalty and political ambition become inextricable as the protagonist rises through the party.
wrongPassages: The two accounts were inextricable: a single audit line separated legitimate expenses from the rest.
She filed an inextricable petition that the court dismissed for lacking any supporting documentation.
Historians praised his inextricable summary for reducing a decade of conflict to a few clear causes.

definition: not in harmony; out of place
memoryTip: In-congruent: doesn’t “fit” the picture; out of place.
correctPassage: The plastic lawn ornaments looked incongruous among the carefully restored Victorian homes.
wrongPassages: Critics called the sequel incongruous because its tone and pacing matched the original exactly.
Her choice of formal attire was incongruous with the black-tie invitation and raised no eyebrows.
The architect praised the new wing as incongruous, noting how seamlessly it continued the older facade.

definition: rude; not showing proper respect
memoryTip: Im-pertinent: not “pertaining” politely — rude and out of line.
correctPassage: The intern’s impertinent interruption of the board chair left the room in stunned silence.
wrongPassages: Colleagues valued her impertinent manner, which never failed to put nervous clients at ease.
The witness gave an impertinent answer that restated the facts without any personal jab.
His impertinent thank-you note carefully acknowledged every person who had helped him.

definition: too great to overcome
memoryTip: Can’t surmount (climb over) it — too big a barrier.
correctPassage: Without additional staffing, the backlog of cases appeared insurmountable before the deadline.
wrongPassages: The team found the final obstacle insurmountable and cleared it in under an hour.
Once the missing file turned up, the earlier confusion proved entirely insurmountable.
She described the short quiz as insurmountable and finished it well before the bell.

definition: the quality of being calm and peaceful
memoryTip: Tranquil + ity — calm lake, quiet mind.
correctPassage: Dawn brought a brief tranquility to the plaza before the weekday crowds arrived.
wrongPassages: The market’s sudden tranquility was measured in triple-digit swings and halted trading.
Neighbors complained that the construction site’s tranquility kept them awake until midnight.
He pursued tranquility by stacking three overlapping deadlines on the same afternoon.

definition: a temporary relief from something unpleasant
memoryTip: A brief relief before the hard thing resumes — temporary break.
correctPassage: A last-minute injunction gave the tenants a brief reprieve from eviction proceedings.
wrongPassages: The manager tried to reprieve late arrivals by docking an hour from each paycheck.
After the final ruling, the court issued a permanent reprieve that closed the case forever.
She called the extended overtime a welcome reprieve from her usual free evenings at home.

definition: not allowing passage; unable to be affected
memoryTip: Im-pervious: nothing can pierce through (water, criticism).
correctPassage: Despite months of public criticism, the committee remained nearly impervious to outside pressure.
wrongPassages: The sandstone was impervious, absorbing the stormwater within minutes of the downpour.
Once the first review appeared, she proved impervious and rewrote every chapter overnight.
He hoped to impervious the jury with a brief, carefully rehearsed opening statement.

definition: not able to be defended or maintained
memoryTip: Can’t tenably hold it — the argument collapses; position is indefensible.
correctPassage: Once the data were corrected, the original hypothesis became untenable.
wrongPassages: After independent replications matched every prediction, the theory looked untenable to reviewers.
Board members called the budget untenable once every line item had clear funding and oversight.
The treaty proved untenable: both sides continued to honor its terms for decades without dispute.

definition: present, appearing, or found everywhere
memoryTip: Ubi = where (Latin) — seems to be everywhere you look.
correctPassage: Smartphones are now so ubiquitous that many public spaces assume constant connectivity.
wrongPassages: The orchid is ubiquitous in the region—only a single wild specimen has ever been documented.
She kept her ubiquitous notes in one locked drawer that no colleague was allowed to open.
After the last factory closed, the brand became ubiquitous on store shelves nationwide.

definition: no longer existing or functioning
memoryTip: De-funct: function stopped — dead, no longer running.
correctPassage: The defunct railway line has been converted into a public walking path.
wrongPassages: The defunct clinic still books appointments daily and posts updated wait times online.
Investors poured capital into the defunct startup after it reported record quarterly growth.
Technicians called the network defunct while monitoring live traffic across every node.

definition: a person who criticizes or disparages someone or something
memoryTip: De-tract: pulls reputation down — a critic who knocks you.
correctPassage: Even the project’s fiercest detractor admitted that the final design was elegant.
wrongPassages: The lead sponsor acted as chief detractor, funding the tour and praising every performance.
She hired a detractor to write the glowing recommendation letter for graduate school.
His lifelong detractor never missed a premiere and always led the standing ovation.

definition: including all possibilities; thorough
memoryTip: Exhausts every option — complete, thorough, nothing left out.
correctPassage: An exhaustive review of the literature found no support for the claim.
wrongPassages: The committee issued an exhaustive statement that addressed only the first of several open questions.
After an exhaustive glance at the abstract, she claimed to have mastered the entire study.
Critics dismissed the audit as exhaustive because it skipped half the departments under review.

definition: diverse in character or content
memoryTip: Hetero = different — a mixed, diverse group.
correctPassage: The sample was deliberately heterogeneous, including rural and urban schools.
wrongPassages: Researchers described the cohort as heterogeneous even though every participant shared the same age, income, and education level.
The alloy was labeled heterogeneous despite consisting of a single pure metal throughout.
Editors praised the anthology’s heterogeneous voice after noticing that every essay repeated the same argument in the same style.

definition: of vital importance; essential
memoryTip: Like an imperative sentence (command) — must-do, essential.
correctPassage: With the storm approaching, it was imperative that residents evacuate promptly.
wrongPassages: Selecting a typeface for the cover letter felt imperative to the success of the clinical trial.
The board treated the optional icebreaker as imperative and canceled the safety briefing instead.

definition: a subtle difference in meaning or expression
memoryTip: A fine shade of meaning — subtle, not black-and-white.
correctPassage: The translation preserved every nuance of the original poem’s tone.
wrongPassages: The campaign’s nuance was a single all-caps slogan designed to be read from a highway billboard.
He reduced the policy debate to a binary choice and called that nuance enough for voters.
Her report captured every nuance by replacing detailed analysis with a yes-or-no checklist.

definition: giving rise to public disagreement
memoryTip: Causes controversy — people argue about it.
correctPassage: The museum’s controversial exhibit drew both praise and protests.
wrongPassages: The controversial ordinance passed unanimously and prompted no public comment whatsoever.

Analysts called the quiet consensus vote controversial after an entirely uneventful session with no dissent.

definition: searching widely for food or provisions
memoryTip: For-aging: out aging in the wild hunting for food.
correctPassage: Along the riverbank, the documentary crew filmed bears foraging for salmon among the rocks.
wrongPassages: The committee spent the morning foraging the budget proposal line by line.
After the storm, the marina looked foraging, with every slip left empty.
She offered a foraging compromise that neither faction would fully accept.

definition: in a way not directly expressed; understood without being stated
memoryTip: Im-plied, not said out loud — understood between the lines.
correctPassage: By remaining silent during the vote, the board implicitly endorsed the chair's decision.
wrongPassages: He answered implicitly by reading every clause of the contract aloud to the room.
She argued implicitly, raising her voice each time a critic interrupted her claim.
The lecturer spoke so implicitly that every syllable was easy to transcribe.

definition: a natural liking or sense of connection
memoryTip: A-finity: a natural 'fit' — you click with someone or something.
correctPassage: She felt an immediate affinity for the spare, geometric style of the paintings.
wrongPassages: Signing the contract created a legal affinity requiring delivery by the end of June.

definition: division into parts; a wall or screen that divides space
memoryTip: Part + ition — splits a whole into parts, or the wall that does it.
correctPassage: A temporary partition divided the gallery into two smaller exhibition rooms.
wrongPassages: Management planned to partition the two research labs into a single shared workspace.

The open floor plan was meant to partition the teams by removing every wall between desks.

definition: very skilled or proficient at something
memoryTip: A-dept: depth of skill — you're really good at it.
correctPassage: She is adept at turning dense research into clear explanations for a general audience.
wrongPassages: The new curriculum was adept from materials the department had used a decade earlier.
After a brief public hearing, the council adept the revised zoning ordinance.
After the festival ended, the empty lot felt strangely adept in the morning light.

definition: cheerfully optimistic, especially in a difficult situation
memoryTip: From Latin sang (blood) — rosy-cheeked and upbeat when things look grim.
correctPassage: Despite repeated setbacks, the director remained sanguine about meeting the opening date.
wrongPassages: Her sanguine memo listed every reason the project was certain to collapse before launch.
After the funding cut, the committee grew sanguine and abandoned any hope of recovery.
The critic’s sanguine review condemned the novel as dull and poorly argued.

definition: existing only in theory or as an idea; hypothetical
memoryTip: Only a notion — theoretical on paper, not yet real.
correctPassage: The budget included only a notional amount for travel until actual costs were known.
wrongPassages: The notional figures were wire-transferred and already spent by Tuesday.
City officials granted a notional license that authorized the restaurant to open at once.

definition: sleepy; tending to induce sleep
memoryTip: Slumber = sleep — anything slumberous makes you drowsy.

wrongPassages: The slumberous finale jolted every listener upright and shouting for an encore.

The slumberous marketplace rang with horns, vendors, and midday traffic.

definition: having the ability to restore health, strength, or well-being
memoryTip: Restores you — rest or care that puts energy back.
correctPassage: A weekend by the lake proved restorative after months of deadline pressure.
wrongPassages: The restorative schedule left the volunteers more depleted than before the break.
Managers scheduled a restorative all-nighter that exhausted the design staff.

definition: to make information known; to give a quality to something
memoryTip: Im-part: pass along a part of knowledge or a quality.

wrongPassages: She chose to impart nothing and sealed the research notes from every colleague.

Inspectors tried to impart a confession from the reluctant witness.

definition: not justified or authorized; lacking good reason
memoryTip: No warrant — no justification; not called for.
correctPassage: The committee dismissed the accusations as unwarranted, noting that the audit had found no irregularities.
wrongPassages: After months of careful review, the board granted her an unwarranted promotion for outstanding results.
The treaty was unwarranted by both nations, who signed it in a public ceremony.
Researchers described the new vaccine as unwarranted because it consistently reduced infection rates.

definition: unreasonably high in price or amount
memoryTip: Ex-orbit: way outside the orbit of a fair price — too high.
correctPassage: Critics argued that the exorbitant tuition left many qualified applicants unable to enroll.
wrongPassages: The library offered exorbitant access to its archives, charging nothing for student cards.
Volunteers agreed that the modest stipend was exorbitant given how little work the role required.
She hoped the exorbitant weather would cool enough for the outdoor ceremony.

definition: to set or mark the boundaries of something
memoryTip: De-mark a line — draw the borders clearly.
correctPassage: The treaty used a river to demarcate the disputed territory between the two provinces.
wrongPassages: The historian tried to demarcate the scandal by refusing to answer any further questions.
Editors asked her to demarcate the draft until every paragraph was vivid and persuasive.

definition: able to be understood; clear enough to grasp
memoryTip: You can 'get' the intelligence of it — understandable.
correctPassage: Once the lecturer slowed her pace, the technical argument became intelligible to the whole class.
wrongPassages: The museum measured each sculpture’s intelligible before deciding where to place it in the gallery.
He preferred films that were deliberately intelligible, full of private jokes no outsider could follow.
The committee voted to intelligible the proposal and send it to the mayor for signature.

definition: careful judgment; freedom to decide as one sees fit
memoryTip: Discreet judgment — careful choice, or the power to choose.
correctPassage: Within the budget ceiling, the principal has discretion to fund programs she considers most urgent.
wrongPassages: The courier delivered the sealed discretion to the clerk and requested a signature.
Bound by a rigid checklist with no exceptions, the clerk exercised broad discretion on every application.
The architect praised the building’s discretion, especially the marble columns along the facade.

definition: modesty; freedom from showiness or pretension
memoryTip: Not pretentious — simple and real, no showing off.
correctPassage: Visitors often credited the gallery's unpretentiousness—bare walls and handwritten labels—for making the art feel approachable.
wrongPassages: His unpretentiousness was on full display in the custom limousine and the security detail at the door.
The awards speech dripped with unpretentiousness as she listed every exclusive honor she had received.
Designers treated unpretentiousness as the season's most extravagant fabric, reserved for red-carpet looks.

definition: to become less intense, severe, or active
memoryTip: Sub + side: sink down — a storm, fever, or anger calms.
correctPassage: Once the fever began to subside, she was able to sleep through the night.
wrongPassages: As the deadline approached, the team's anxiety only seemed to subside with every new complication.

definition: a mischievous practical joke
memoryTip: A playful trick — fun until someone gets hurt or mad.
correctPassage: What started as a harmless prank escalated into a costly misunderstanding.
wrongPassages: The board approved the five-year budget prank after independent auditors reviewed every line.
Her promotion was widely described as a prank for a decade of careful, unglamorous work.
Researchers called the new treatment a medical prank that could sharply reduce hospital stays.

definition: to show or reveal a quality, feeling, or trait clearly
memoryTip: E-vince like evidence — it shows a quality is there.
correctPassage: The early drafts already evince the precision that would mark her mature style.
wrongPassages: She hoped a clearer presentation would finally evince the skeptical committee to fund the study.
The sealed files were meant to evince the controversy from journalists for as long as possible.

definition: to make impossible; to prevent from happening
memoryTip: Pre-clude: close the door in advance — make it impossible.
correctPassage: A prior commitment precludes her from joining the evening session.
wrongPassages: The open forum was designed to preclude neighbors who had felt shut out of earlier planning meetings.
Her brief remarks will preclude the keynote and establish the themes for the rest of the day.
Flexible office hours preclude students who need help outside the standard schedule.

definition: situated at the back; later in time
memoryTip: Post = after/behind — rear end of the body, or what comes later.
correctPassage: In the diagram, the posterior section of the brain is shaded in blue.
wrongPassages: She reserved the posterior seats near the stage so the audience would see her first.
Archaeologists labeled the earliest layer posterior because it was deposited before all others.
The committee made the posterior announcement at the start of the meeting, ahead of every other item.

definition: a formal written request; to make such a request
memoryTip: A formal “please” on paper — you petition for action, not for fun.
correctPassage: Residents signed a petition asking the city to restore weekend bus service.
wrongPassages: The judge issued a petition ordering the company to halt construction at once.
Researchers published a petition summarizing three years of climate measurements.
She petitioned the whiteboard with lecture notes before the students arrived.

definition: required by law or rules; compulsory
memoryTip: Mandate = command — if it’s mandatory, skipping it isn’t allowed.
correctPassage: Safety training is mandatory for everyone who enters the laboratory.
wrongPassages: Parking in the fire lane is mandatory under the city’s traffic rules.
The workshop was mandatory, so volunteers could skip it without consequence.
After a social-media trend, the novel became mandatory among teenagers who simply preferred it.

definition: allowed; permitted under the rules
memoryTip: You have permission — permissible means it’s okay to do.
correctPassage: Under the new rules, only certain additives are permissible in the product.
wrongPassages: Driving through a red light is permissible under standard traffic law.
Reviewers called the staging permissible, the finest production of the year.
They drafted a permissible contract that neither side could ever revise or cancel.

definition: dependent on something else; a group representing a larger body
memoryTip: Tied to a contingency — it happens only if X happens first.
correctPassage: Approval is contingent on the environmental review being completed on time.
wrongPassages: Funding was contingent and required no conditions of any kind.

definition: use up or greatly reduce the supply of
memoryTip: De-plete (empty the plate) — drain the stock until little is left.
correctPassage: Continued drought threatened to deplete the aquifer that supplies the valley's farms.
wrongPassages: Donors hoped to deplete the empty scholarship fund with a multiyear gift.

Volunteers worked overnight to deplete shelves left bare by the storm.

definition: comply with rules, standards, or prevailing norms
memoryTip: Con-form: take the same form as the rules or the group.
correctPassage: All packaging must conform to the new labeling regulations before shipment.
wrongPassages: She was praised for refusing to conform when she adopted the dress code without complaint.
The architect redesigned the wing to conform by discarding every clause of the building code.

definition: basic; involving only the simplest principles
memoryTip: Rude / raw basics — only the first, simplest steps, not advanced.
correctPassage: Even a rudimentary grasp of statistics helps readers evaluate misleading graphs.
wrongPassages: Her rudimentary dissertation synthesized decades of specialized research across three fields.
The hospital reserved its most rudimentary instruments for the complex transplant.
Reviewers called the treatise rudimentary, citing its exhaustive treatment of every major theory.

definition: scarcity; smallness of number or amount
memoryTip: Pauc- = few (Latin) — a paucity means not many, almost none.
correctPassage: A paucity of eyewitness accounts left investigators with little to go on.
wrongPassages: Critics noted a paucity of talent on a roster stacked with award winners.

After days of rain, a paucity of water stood several feet deep in the streets.

definition: the appearance of being true or real
memoryTip: Veri (truth) + similar — looks true-to-life, even if it's fiction.
correctPassage: Careful attention to period speech lends the drama a striking verisimilitude.
wrongPassages: The abstract canvas was praised for the photographic verisimilitude of its blank color fields.
She achieved verisimilitude by inventing sources no researcher could verify.
The farce's slapstick chaos was celebrated for its documentary verisimilitude.

definition: find out for certain; determine
memoryTip: As-certain: make it certain — dig until you know for sure.
correctPassage: Investigators sought to ascertain whether the signal was natural or artificial.
wrongPassages: Without consulting the archives, the historian simply ascertained that the treaty had never been signed.

Several witnesses ascertained colorful details that later proved to have no basis in the record.

definition: provide evidence to support a claim
memoryTip: Give the claim substance — back it up with proof, not vibes.
correctPassage: Without field measurements, the team could not substantiate its claim.
wrongPassages: He tried to substantiate the charge by discarding every document that might contradict it.
The essay substantiated its thesis merely by restating the claim in more emphatic language.
Editors asked her to substantiate the article by stripping out the footnotes and source notes.

definition: remarkably great in size, amount, or degree
memoryTip: Prodigy-level scale — so large or impressive it stands out.
correctPassage: The archive preserves a prodigious number of letters from the period.
wrongPassages: After years of study he showed only a prodigious grasp of the material, stumbling over basic terms.
The museum devoted a prodigious gallery to a single postage-stamp-sized watercolor.
Critics called the reform package prodigious, noting that it altered only one minor administrative rule.

definition: involving deceit; obtained or done by deception
memoryTip: Fraud — dishonest, fake, or won by tricking someone.
correctPassage: Auditors uncovered fraudulent invoices submitted by a subcontractor.
wrongPassages: Reviewers dismissed the thoroughly sourced study as fraudulent after confirming each cited reference.
Her fraudulent disclosure listed every asset exactly as the filing rules required.
The firm’s fraudulent ledgers balanced because each transaction was recorded under accepted standards.

definition: able to be touched or felt; so intense as to seem tangible
memoryTip: You can almost palm it — so clear or strong you can feel it.
correctPassage: Tension in the room was palpable as the results were announced.
wrongPassages: The discrepancy between the two drafts was so palpable that careful readers failed to notice it.
A palpable hush filled the stadium once the crowd began cheering at full volume.
Administrators tried to palpable the complaints by removing the public comment form.

definition: cause surprise or confusion; mix up or thwart
memoryTip: Con-found: throw into confusion — mix up or leave people stunned.
correctPassage: The experiment’s results continued to confound researchers who had predicted a simpler pattern.
wrongPassages: A careful chronology helped confound the sequence of events for the investigating panel.
She hoped the abstract would confound her thesis by restating each claim in plainer language.
New measurements confound the earlier study by reproducing its main findings almost exactly.

definition: pay no attention to; ignore
memoryTip: Dis + regard — drop your regard; treat it as if it doesn’t matter.
correctPassage: Critics accused the agency of disregard for the community’s documented concerns.
wrongPassages: Her disregard for the sources meant she checked every citation before the article went to press.
The board’s disregard for the proposal involved weeks of debate and a full public hearing.
Students showed disregard for the assignment by submitting detailed drafts well ahead of the deadline.

definition: emphasize or draw attention to
memoryTip: Like underlining a line — you underscore what matters most.
correctPassage: The new findings underscore the need for longer-term studies of the treatment.
wrongPassages: He underscored the conclusion by omitting it from the final presentation entirely.
The footnote underscored the claim by questioning every piece of supporting evidence.
Editors underscored the story’s importance by moving it to a less prominent section.

definition: conforming to traditional or established doctrine
memoryTip: Ortho = straight — by-the-book, traditional belief or method.
correctPassage: Her approach departed from orthodox methods that the field had relied on for decades.
wrongPassages: His orthodox redesign rejected every convention the profession still treated as standard.
Critics called the film orthodox for abandoning the genre’s familiar narrative structure.
She followed an orthodox training plan built only from experimental techniques no coach had tried.

definition: the highest point; peak of power or success
memoryTip: Highest point in the sky — and the peak of a career or empire.
correctPassage: The empire reached its zenith under the second emperor’s long and stable rule.
wrongPassages: The firm reached its zenith the year losses forced a major restructuring of the company.
At the zenith of the dig, crews finally exposed the lowest foundation stones of the fort.
Historians place the movement’s zenith in the obscure years before it gained any public following.

definition: great size, extent, or importance
memoryTip: Think magnum (huge bottle) — magnitude is how big or important something is.
correctPassage: Few grasped the magnitude of the crisis until the independent audit was released.
wrongPassages: Reviewers praised the magnitude of the essay for its delicate understatement and brevity.
She measured the magnitude of the rumor by how few people had even heard of it.
The magnitude of his courtesy was noted mainly in how rarely he held open a door.

definition: be a perfect example of
memoryTip: Epitome = the perfect example; to epitomize is to be that example.
correctPassage: The building’s spare lines epitomize mid-century modern design.
wrongPassages: His rambling digressions epitomize the concise brief the client had requested.
The shuttered warehouse epitomizes the city’s widely celebrated revitalization.
Her reluctance to speak epitomized the decisive leadership the board expected.

definition: failure to meet an obligation; or a preselected option
memoryTip: If you don’t choose, you get the default — the fallback (or you fail to pay).
correctPassage: If no option is selected, the software applies a conservative default setting.
wrongPassages: She defaulted on the loan by sending every installment well before it was due.
The program’s default forced users to configure dozens of options before any work began.
His default reply was reinvented from scratch for each nearly identical request.

definition: unnecessary; more than what is needed
memoryTip: Super + flow — overflow you don’t need; extra fluff to cut.
correctPassage: Editors cut superfluous adjectives that lengthened the prose without adding clarity.
wrongPassages: The surgeon called the monitor superfluous while relying on it throughout the procedure.
On a long desert crossing, water proved superfluous once the heat grew severe.
Instructors labeled the practice exams superfluous after only those who took them improved.

definition: the quality of being exact; precision
memoryTip: Exact + -itude — the state of being exact; pure precision.
correctPassage: Cartography of that era prized exactitude over decorative flourish.
wrongPassages: He prized exactitude in estimates that swung wildly from one meeting to the next.
Her exactitude with sources left several key citations missing or incomplete.
They pursued exactitude by rounding every figure to the nearest order of magnitude.

definition: cause or give rise to
memoryTip: En-gender: “give birth to” an idea, feeling, or result — cause it.
correctPassage: Sudden cuts to research funding can engender resentment among scientists mid-project.
wrongPassages: Diplomats stayed late in order to engender the last remnants of the border dispute.
He engendered the family firm from his uncle and sold it within a year.
The crew engendered the storm for six hours before the engines finally failed.

definition: officially assign a status, role, or name
memoryTip: De-sign it as official — name or assign a role on purpose.
correctPassage: The board will designate a temporary chair until formal elections can be held.
wrongPassages: The architect spent weeks designating the façade in charcoal before any concrete was poured.
After the inquiry, she designated her post and left the agency without comment.
Judges designated the winning entry by declining to name any finalist at all.

definition: make an unpleasant feeling less intense
memoryTip: Sounds like “a suage / soothe age of pain” — ease a bad feeling.
correctPassage: Nothing in the briefing could assuage investors’ fears about the product recall.
wrongPassages: Commentators rushed to assuage the controversy with still sharper public accusations.
Analysts met before the hearing to assuage the quarterly figures line by line.
She agreed to assuage full responsibility for the missed deadline.

definition: a made-up falsehood; or the act of manufacturing
memoryTip: Fabricated like fake cloth — a made-up story (or something manufactured).
correctPassage: Investigators concluded that the signature on the form was a fabrication.
wrongPassages: Editors praised her fabrication of the timeline for matching every court record exactly.
Their fabrication on the paper earned both coauthors equal credit in the journal.
Demolition crews finished the fabrication of the old wing before noon.

definition: sincere and serious in intention
memoryTip: In earnest — sincere, not joking; you really mean it.
correctPassage: Her earnest appeal for more lab time persuaded even the skeptical dean.
wrongPassages: He offered an earnest quip that left the room laughing and the issue forgotten.
With an earnest glance at her phone, she promised help and never followed up.
They dismissed the proposal as too earnest for the department’s limited budget.

definition: dwell unhappily on a thought; also a group of young birds
memoryTip: Like a hen brooding — sit and stew on dark thoughts (or a clutch of chicks).
correctPassage: He continued to brood over the failed trial long after the rest of the team had moved on.
wrongPassages: She brooded over the invitation by accepting it at once and arriving early to help set up.
Once the problem was solved, they brooded cheerfully over their success around the table.
The panel brooded the agenda item for two minutes, then approved it without further comment.

definition: deep respect, often tinged with awe
memoryTip: Revere someone — treat them with deep, almost sacred respect.
correctPassage: Visitors approached the manuscript with a reverence reserved for rare and fragile objects.
wrongPassages: Critics praised his reverence for the score, which he rearranged freely without consulting the original markings.
The class showed reverence for the guest lecturer by talking through most of her presentation.
She expressed reverence for the collection by handling the oldest volumes without gloves.

definition: serving as a desirable model; outstandingly good
memoryTip: Worthy to be an example — model behavior others should copy.
correctPassage: Her laboratory notebooks are exemplary in their clarity and care.
wrongPassages: Reviewers called the draft exemplary, citing its incomplete citations and unsupported claims.
His exemplary attendance record listed more absences than any other student in the course.
The board held up the delayed, over-budget project as exemplary of how future initiatives should run.

definition: openly resist or refuse to obey; go against
memoryTip: De-fy: refuse to bow — openly resist an order or expectation.
correctPassage: The results appear to defy the predictions of the standard model.
wrongPassages: She chose to defy the curfew by returning home well before the deadline each night.
The class decided to defy the instructor by following the assigned outline section by section.
He managed to defy the ban by securing every required permit before the event began.

definition: important or relevant (as in material evidence)
memoryTip: Matters materially — important/relevant, not just “stuff” you can touch.
correctPassage: Only material differences between the samples were reported in the abstract.
wrongPassages: The judge called the typo material to the verdict, noting that it changed nothing about the evidence.
Counsel argued that a material fact was one the jury could safely set aside.
Researchers labeled the discrepancy material precisely because it had no bearing on the conclusions.

definition: ability to stretch and resume shape; adaptability
memoryTip: Like elastic — stretches and snaps back; also flexible response to change.
correctPassage: The market showed surprising elasticity as consumers adjusted quickly to the sudden rise in prices.
wrongPassages: The department’s elasticity showed in its refusal to alter any procedure after the new rules took effect.
Critics praised his elasticity of mind for rejecting every alternative without a second look.
Once stretched past its limit, the material’s elasticity left it permanently deformed and unable to recover.

definition: a scarcity or lack of something
memoryTip: Sounds like “death of supply” — a serious lack or shortage.
correctPassage: A dearth of qualified applicants delayed the hire for months.
wrongPassages: A dearth of volunteers filled every available shift well ahead of the deadline.
Farmers celebrated a dearth of rainfall that left reservoirs above capacity for the first time in years.
The library’s dearth of new titles forced an expansion of the stacks to house the surplus.

definition: make something seem less important than it is
memoryTip: Play it down — shrink how big or serious something sounds.
correctPassage: Officials tried to downplay the severity of the shortage in their public statements.
wrongPassages: She downplayed the award by arranging extensive coverage and a formal reception in her honor.
They downplayed the risk by printing large warnings on every package the company sold.
He downplayed the scandal by giving reporters a detailed timeline of every disputed decision.

definition: surpass; go beyond or move faster than
memoryTip: Strip ahead of the pack — run past and leave others behind.
correctPassage: Demand continues to outstrip the region’s ability to supply housing.
wrongPassages: Sales outstripped the forecast by falling short of the target every quarter.
Her pace outstripped the field when she finished several minutes behind the leaders.
Junior staff outstripped senior analysts by needing substantially more supervision on each project.

definition: tendency to stay unchanged; resistance to a change in motion
memoryTip: Newton’s inertia — stays still (or keeps going) until something pushes it.
correctPassage: Institutional inertia made reforming the curriculum slow and difficult.
wrongPassages: The startup’s inertia was evident in its weekly product redesigns and shifting strategy.
Her inertia showed as she revised the proposal three times before the morning meeting ended.
Market inertia kept prices swinging sharply with each new rumor throughout the session.

definition: the state of being everywhere at once
memoryTip: Ubi (Latin “where”) + everywhere — so common it’s hard to escape.
correctPassage: The ubiquity of online databases has reshaped how historians locate primary sources.
wrongPassages: Scholars prized the manuscript’s ubiquity, since only a single copy had survived the fire.
A ubiquity of qualified specialists forced the clinic to turn patients away for months.
After the outage, the ubiquity of reliable connectivity left the team unable to share files.

definition: not harmful or offensive; harmless
memoryTip: In- (not) + noxious (harmful) — a remark that doesn’t sting.
correctPassage: Reviewers judged the dye innocuous at the concentrations used in the clinical trials.
wrongPassages: The innocuous spill required full evacuation of the laboratory and a hazmat response.
Diplomats called the remark innocuous after it nearly collapsed the negotiations.
Doctors warned that the innocuous compound could cause permanent nerve damage if ingested.

definition: extremely complex and difficult to follow
memoryTip: Think of a volume coiled into tight twists — overly complex.
correctPassage: The statute’s convoluted language left lower courts divided over its intended scope.
wrongPassages: Her convoluted summary reduced the entire debate to a single transparent claim.
The trail was convoluted: one unmarked straight path from the gate to the overlook.
He gave a convoluted reply that named the core problem in the opening sentence.

definition: most noticeable or important; standing out
memoryTip: From Latin salire, “to leap” — points that leap out at you.
correctPassage: Among several results, the most salient was the unexpected rise in retention rates.
wrongPassages: The team treated the salient findings as minor footnotes unlikely to affect the conclusion.
She ranked a small typo as the report’s most salient flaw and set aside the sampling error.
His salient contribution was so slight that colleagues forgot he had joined the project.

definition: to prevent someone from accomplishing something
memoryTip: A thwart is a cross-seat in a boat — something that blocks your path.
correctPassage: Strict export rules may thwart researchers’ efforts to share the dataset internationally.
wrongPassages: The grant was designed to thwart the study by covering equipment, travel, and staff time.
Early feedback helped thwart the proposal by clarifying weak sections before submission.
The new route will thwart delivery delays by adding direct service between the two hubs.

definition: to delay or block by creating an obstacle
memoryTip: Im-pede: put something in the path of the feet — slow progress.
correctPassage: Construction along the highway will impede delivery trucks until the detour opens next month.
wrongPassages: Additional funding will impede the research team’s ability to finish the study on schedule.
The new software is designed to impede workflow by automating the most time-consuming steps.
Mentors impede first-year students by helping them navigate registration and course selection.

definition: to gather information bit by bit from various sources
memoryTip: Farmers glean leftover grain — pick up scraps of info the same way.
correctPassage: From scattered field notes, the biologist could glean how the bird population had shifted over decades.
wrongPassages: She chose to glean the entire archive in a single uninterrupted afternoon of reading.
Investigators gleaned the missing motive by inventing details no witness had supplied.
Administrators chose to glean the controversial passage by deleting it from the final report.

definition: lasting only a very short time
memoryTip: Ephemera once meant “for a day” — here today, gone tomorrow.
correctPassage: The desert bloom is ephemeral, vanishing within days once the rains end.
wrongPassages: Stone monuments are ephemeral because they outlast the civilizations that raised them.
Their ephemeral collaboration has produced books together for more than thirty years.
He filed the ephemeral records in a permanent archive meant to preserve them indefinitely.

definition: occasionally; at irregular intervals
memoryTip: In scattered spots — now and then, not on a steady schedule.
correctPassage: The rare bird appears only sporadically along this stretch of coast.
wrongPassages: The factory whistle blew sporadically at the same minute every morning without fail.
She practiced sporadically: two hours each day for six months without missing a session.
Trains arrived sporadically according to a published timetable that never varied.

definition: filled with something undesirable; tense with risk
memoryTip: Freighted with trouble — loaded down with tension or danger.
correctPassage: The negotiations were fraught with misunderstandings from the first meeting.
wrongPassages: Their vacation was fraught with calm beaches and uninterrupted sleep.
The simple recipe was fraught with only three ingredients and one pan.
He found the empty hallway fraught with silence and free of any tension.

definition: in a way that suggests a favorable outcome
memoryTip: Auspicious omens once came from watching birds — a promising start.
correctPassage: The campaign opened auspiciously, drawing record attendance and early endorsements.
wrongPassages: Negotiations began auspiciously when both sides walked out after ten minutes.
The harvest started auspiciously under a late frost that ruined the first crop.
Critics took the empty house on opening night as an auspiciously promising sign.

definition: in a random, unplanned, or careless way
memoryTip: Hap (chance) + hazard — by luck, not by plan; messy.
correctPassage: Evidence had been filed haphazardly, so researchers spent weeks reconstructing the timeline.
wrongPassages: The archivist arranged the letters haphazardly by date, sender, and subject.
She packed haphazardly, numbering each carton and checking items against a list.
The drill team advanced haphazardly in precise formation across the field.

definition: showing opposition or hostility
memoryTip: Like a story’s antagonist — opposing, not cooperative.
correctPassage: The two accounts need not be antagonistic; each explains a different stage of the process.
wrongPassages: Her antagonistic remarks quickly put the room at ease.
The firms signed an antagonistic partnership to share costs and profits.
Residents organized an antagonistic welcome dinner for the new neighbors.

definition: a summary; the act of adding things up
memoryTip: Sum it up — a total or a closing overview.
correctPassage: In her summation, the author restated the study’s main findings without adding new data.
wrongPassages: His summation introduced entirely new evidence and abandoned any closing overview.
The report’s summation scattered unfinished notes instead of drawing the claims together.
She began the talk with a summation that postponed any review until the final slide.

definition: leaving no doubt; clear and unambiguous
memoryTip: Un-equi-vocal: not two voices — one clear meaning only.
correctPassage: The committee issued an unequivocal statement endorsing the revised policy.
wrongPassages: His unequivocal reply was that the outcome might change under several unknowns.
The instructions were unequivocal: three conflicting steps and no final choice.
She offered an unequivocal shrug that left the panel more uncertain than before.

definition: beyond criticism; faultless
memoryTip: You can’t reproach (blame) them — conduct with no fault to find.
correctPassage: Colleagues described her handling of the inquiry as irreproachable from start to finish.
wrongPassages: The inspector labeled the firm’s record irreproachable after listing a dozen safety violations.
His irreproachable testimony was dismissed once several clear contradictions emerged.
Reviewers found the manuscript irreproachable, citing careless sourcing and unfinished arguments.

definition: relating to mental links or connections between ideas
memoryTip: Works by association — memory links, not strict step-by-step logic.
correctPassage: The poem moves by associative leaps, linking images that share tone rather than plot.
wrongPassages: Her associative outline kept each claim isolated so no idea could connect to the next.
The lab preferred associative procedures that followed a fixed sequence with no room for linked ideas.
He praised the report’s associative structure: every paragraph stood alone, free of cross-reference.

definition: impossible to avoid or resist
memoryTip: In-e-luctable: you can’t struggle free — the outcome is locked in.
correctPassage: Under current emissions paths, climate models project ineluctable warming over the coming decades.
wrongPassages: She treated the deadline as ineluctable and simply postponed the project another month.
Once the detour opened, the traffic jam proved ineluctable and drivers slipped past easily.
Voters found the tax measure ineluctable, so they rejected it and adopted a milder plan.

definition: very weak, thin, or slight
memoryTip: Thin as a tenuous thread — a weak link that may snap.
correctPassage: The link between the two studies remains tenuous and should not be overstated.
wrongPassages: Their tenuous alliance has weathered three decades of crisis without strain.
She assembled a tenuous case built on undisputed records and consistent witness accounts.
Engineers called the bridge’s supports tenuous, confident the structure would last a century.

definition: to fail by trying to do or control too much
memoryTip: Reach too far — stretch beyond your power and fall short.
correctPassage: Critics accused the agency of regulatory overreach into decisions better left to local governments.
wrongPassages: The careful budget showed overreach by keeping every expense well below the approved limit.
Colleagues praised her modest aims as overreach after she declined several ambitious projects.
With limited staff, their overreach meant finishing only what they could complete thoroughly.

definition: make narrower by squeezing
memoryTip: Con-strict: squeeze tight like a constrictor snake.
correctPassage: Cold can constrict blood vessels near the skin, reducing heat loss from the body.
wrongPassages: Engineers plan to constrict the tunnel by widening it to four lanes of traffic.
The reforms will constrict competition by removing licensing barriers for new firms.
She tried to constrict the tight deadline by adding two extra weeks to the schedule.

definition: match or surpass by imitation
memoryTip: E-mulate: imitate to equal or beat someone you admire.
correctPassage: Young designers often try to emulate the restraint of mid-century masters.
wrongPassages: She chose to emulate the mentor by ignoring every technique the mentor had used.
Critics hope the studio will emulate the hit film by inventing a story with no shared elements.
He tried to emulate the outdated methods by discarding them entirely in favor of new ones.

definition: make greater by adding to
memoryTip: Aug-ment: add more; make something greater.
correctPassage: Grants will augment the school’s own funding for after-school programs.
wrongPassages: The board voted to augment the budget by cutting every discretionary line item.
Managers plan to augment staffing by freezing all hiring through the next fiscal year.
She hoped to augment the sparse collection by returning several volumes to the donor.

definition: leave a place previously occupied
memoryTip: Leave it vacant — empty the place and go.
correctPassage: Tenants were ordered to vacate the building within thirty days.
wrongPassages: The firm will vacate the office by moving additional staff into the same suite.
He refused to vacate the apartment and signed a three-year extension instead.
Organizers plan to vacate the hall by packing every available seat before the doors open.

definition: extend conclusions beyond known data
memoryTip: Extra + polate: push the pattern past the data you have.
correctPassage: It is risky to extrapolate from such a small sample to the whole population.
wrongPassages: She refused to extrapolate, reporting only results that fell inside the measured range.
They chose to extrapolate the dataset by discarding every observation past the first year.
He tried to extrapolate the trend by averaging only the known points and stopping there.

definition: come or bring together for a meeting
memoryTip: Con-vene: come together for a meeting.
correctPassage: The board will convene next Monday to vote on the proposal.
wrongPassages: Managers convened the staff by sending everyone home early and locking the offices.
The mediator convened the talks by canceling the remaining sessions without notice.
She convened the coalition by dissolving it into separate, noncommunicating factions.

definition: so lacking in originality as to be boring
memoryTip: So common it bans all interest — boringly ordinary.
correctPassage: What might have been a powerful speech was undermined by banal slogans.
wrongPassages: Critics praised the film’s banal plot for inventing a structure no prior director had tried.
Her banal theorem introduced an entirely new branch of mathematics almost overnight.
Reviewers called the novel banal because every chapter broke with convention in unexpected ways.

definition: not even or regular in pattern; unpredictable
memoryTip: Err + path: jumps around without a steady pattern.
correctPassage: Erratic attendance made it hard to keep the seminar on schedule.
wrongPassages: Astronomers call a star erratic when its brightness never changes across decades.
She kept an erratic schedule: the same three tasks at the same times each day.
His erratic explanation listed steps in order with diagrams and a glossary for every term.

definition: not candid or sincere; falsely appearing frank
memoryTip: Dis + ingenuous (innocent) — fake sincerity, not genuine.
correctPassage: Claiming surprise at the outcome seemed disingenuous after months of warnings.
wrongPassages: Colleagues trusted her disingenuous account because she documented every step without concealment.
His disingenuous apology named every harm, accepted full blame, and offered a concrete remedy.
Judges called the ruling disingenuous because it carefully weighed both sides and cited the law.

definition: waver between different opinions or actions
memoryTip: Vacillate like a vacuum of decision — swing back and forth.
correctPassage: Investors continue to vacillate between optimism and caution.
wrongPassages: They vacillated on the first vote: every hand went up at once with no further discussion.
She vacillated between options by locking in her first choice and never revisiting it.
His vacillating leadership held a single, unchanging course for the entire term.

definition: inflict serious damage on; disfigure
memoryTip: Mutilate = maim: seriously harm or disfigure something.
correctPassage: The fire mutilated several rare manuscripts before firefighters contained the blaze.
wrongPassages: Conservators carefully mutilated the fresco so that later visitors could appreciate its original colors.
The editor asked the author to mutilate a few sentences for clarity without changing the argument.
After negotiations, the two companies agreed to mutilate their dispute and resume joint research.

definition: innocent and unsuspecting; candidly naive
memoryTip: In-genuous: genuine innocence — not scheming (not ingenious!).
correctPassage: His ingenuous trust in the brochure left him unprepared for the hidden fees.
wrongPassages: The lobbyist’s ingenuous strategy used shell companies and deliberately vague disclosures.
An ingenuous cover story, rehearsed for months, convinced even the skeptical investigators.
She was praised as an ingenuous bargainer who outmaneuvered rivals with careful misdirection.

definition: clever, original, and inventive
memoryTip: In-genius: clever invention (don’t confuse with ingenuous!).
correctPassage: An ingenious filtration design allowed the remote clinic to reuse limited water safely.
wrongPassages: Reviewers called the proposal ingenious because it restated last year’s plan without a single change.
Colleagues called the form ingenious even though it asked only for a name and a signature.
The witness gave an ingenious account, candidly admitting she had noticed almost nothing of the incident.

definition: not showing care for the consequences of an action
memoryTip: Im-prudent: not prudent — careless about consequences.
correctPassage: Expanding the plant without stress-testing the supply chain struck many analysts as imprudent.
wrongPassages: The committee praised the imprudent budget for building reserves and deferring nonessential spending.
Her imprudent decision followed months of scenario planning and independent legal review.
Judges called the ruling imprudent because it carefully weighed both sides and cited settled precedent.

definition: be a sign or warning of (a future event)
memoryTip: Pre-sage: a sign before the event — an omen.
correctPassage: A sudden drop in overnight temperatures seemed to presage an early frost.
wrongPassages: The historian used new archival letters to presage what had already happened a century earlier.
After the treaty was signed, diplomats gathered to presage the outcome they had just secured.
The report did not presage any future risk; it merely listed last quarter’s completed projects.

definition: prevent from speaking freely
memoryTip: Like a dog’s muzzle — silence or restrain speech.
correctPassage: Attempts to muzzle dissenting scientists only increased public suspicion.
wrongPassages: Editors hoped to muzzle the controversy by giving every critic a full column to respond.
She tried to muzzle the inquiry by releasing the complete transcript the same afternoon.
The board moved to muzzle the whistleblower by promoting her to a more public role.

definition: not producing the desired effect
memoryTip: In-effectual: has no real effect; doesn’t work.
correctPassage: The half-hearted apology was ineffectual in calming the controversy.
wrongPassages: Her ineffectual treatment cleared every symptom within forty-eight hours.
The campaign proved ineffectual: turnout rose sharply and the measure passed by a wide margin.
Analysts called the intervention ineffectual precisely because it achieved every stated goal.

definition: undermine the power or authority of
memoryTip: Sub + vert: overturn from below — undermine authority.
correctPassage: Satire can subvert official narratives by exposing their contradictions.
wrongPassages: The reforms were designed to subvert authoritarian rule by expanding voting access and oversight.
They hoped to subvert the constitution by enforcing its amendments more strictly.
She sought to subvert the chair’s authority by carefully following every rule the chair had set.

definition: assuming power without justification; arrogantly domineering
memoryTip: Imperial attitude — bossy, assuming command without right.
correctPassage: His imperious tone made collaboration with junior staff difficult.
wrongPassages: Her imperious manner put everyone at ease and invited open disagreement.
Colleagues praised his imperious style for never issuing orders and always asking first.
The director’s imperious request for feedback made the junior writers feel free to challenge her draft.

definition: small or insufficient in quantity
memoryTip: Scant = barely enough — too little of something.
correctPassage: Evidence for the theory remains scanty and contested.
wrongPassages: The harvest was scanty: silos overflowed and crews still left grain in the fields.
Her scanty briefing covered risks, costs, and a recommendation across four full slides.
Researchers called the data set scanty after every variable had been measured in triplicate.

definition: interpret wrongly; misunderstand
memoryTip: Mis + construe (build meaning) — you build the wrong meaning from what was said.
correctPassage: Critics warned that readers might misconstrue the satire as a literal policy proposal.
wrongPassages: The historian carefully misconstrued each primary source before drawing her conclusions.
She misconstrued the instructions so precisely that the experiment ran without error.
A skilled diplomat can misconstrue a rival's position and still negotiate in good faith.

definition: criticize unfairly; belittle
memoryTip: De-nigrate: blacken someone's name — smear them with unfair criticism.
correctPassage: Some commentators denigrate the entire reform effort over a single procedural delay.
wrongPassages: The committee denigrated the proposal by awarding it the top research prize.
Mentors often denigrate young scholars by highlighting their strongest contributions.
She denigrated the novel in a review that praised its structure and insight.

definition: make void or cancel out
memoryTip: Make null — cancel it so it no longer counts or has force.
correctPassage: The amendment was written to nullify earlier clauses that conflicted with new law.
wrongPassages: Additional funding will nullify the project by securing its long-term survival.
The court nullified the statute by reaffirming that it remains fully enforceable.
She nullified the agreement by signing every remaining section without change.

definition: irrelevant or unrelated to the matter at hand
memoryTip: Extra stuff that doesn't belong — noise outside the real point.
correctPassage: The editor removed extraneous examples that distracted from the main claim.
wrongPassages: The extraneous premise was the one claim on which the whole argument rested.
Jurors treated the extraneous testimony as decisive proof of the defendant's guilt.
Her extraneous outline listed only the steps the research team actually needed.

definition: collect or form into a mass or cluster
memoryTip: Ag-glomerate like glue — bits clump into one sticky mass.
correctPassage: Fine mineral grains can agglomerate into denser deposits along river bends.
wrongPassages: The chemist waited for the solute to agglomerate until no solid remained in solution.
Organizers agglomerated the audience by opening extra doors and thinning the crowd.
She agglomerated the long report by cutting it from forty pages to a brief summary.

definition: situated at the front; earlier in time
memoryTip: Ante = before — the front side, or what came earlier.
correctPassage: The surgeon marked the incision along the anterior surface of the thigh.
wrongPassages: From the rear of the auditorium, she had a clear anterior view of the stage.
The sequel, released years later, was described as anterior to the original film.
The revised conclusion, written last, was labeled the anterior section of the paper.

definition: gather or accumulate in large amount
memoryTip: A-mass: pile up a mass of something over time.
correctPassage: Over decades the archive amassed one of the region’s most complete sets of wartime letters.
wrongPassages: The collector amassed the collection by selling every rare piece within a week.
She amassed the debt by clearing every balance the day each statement arrived.
The laboratory amassed its samples by discarding any specimen that failed inspection.

definition: agree; occur at the same time
memoryTip: Con-cur: run together — same opinion, or same moment.
correctPassage: Most historians concur that the reform had a larger effect than its authors expected.
wrongPassages: The two committees concurred by issuing sharply opposed recommendations.
She concurred the locked laboratory door with a brief note left for the staff.
Reviewers called the recovery concur once the patient was discharged the same day.

definition: intervene on behalf of another
memoryTip: Inter + cede: step between parties and plead for someone.
correctPassage: A respected diplomat offered to intercede with the board on the students’ behalf.
wrongPassages: Rather than plead for leniency, the lawyer interceded by urging a harsher penalty.
She interceded her own promotion without once referring to a colleague’s case.
Editors labeled the chapter intercede after it introduced every specialized term.

definition: a small improvement; elegance or polish
memoryTip: Make finer — polish the details until it feels elegant.
correctPassage: A final refinement of the algorithm reduced error rates without slowing the system.
wrongPassages: The rough outline was already a refinement of the polished final manuscript.
They stored the refinement in a drawer beside spare cables and blank forms.
His refinement of the proposal stripped out every improvement and restored earlier flaws.

definition: a shared feature or attribute
memoryTip: What is common to both — a feature they share.
correctPassage: Despite cultural differences, researchers found a surprising commonality in how children learn numbers.
wrongPassages: Survey results revealed a striking commonality: respondents agreed on almost none of the questions.
The report stressed a commonality that made each region’s economy distinct from all the others.
Linguists found little commonality between the dialects, which shared nearly identical grammar and vocabulary.

definition: strong hostility or ill will
memoryTip: Animus = hostile spirit — deep dislike, not mild annoyance.
correctPassage: Years of rivalry had produced deep animosity between the neighboring towns.
wrongPassages: Long collaboration left an animosity that made the partners eager to work together again.
Her animosity toward the mentor was plain in the gratitude she expressed at every ceremony.
The treaty was signed amid animosity so warm that both sides hosted joint celebrations for weeks.

definition: an abundance or large quantity
memoryTip: Pro-fusion: pour forth in abundance — almost too much.
correctPassage: Spring brought a profusion of wildflowers to the hillside.
wrongPassages: A profusion of applications left the committee with almost no candidates to consider.
After the drought, farmers noted a profusion of crops that barely filled a single wagon.
The archive’s profusion of documents meant researchers found almost nothing on the subject.

definition: cancel out; make ineffective
memoryTip: Make it negative — wipe out the force of a claim or effect.
correctPassage: One contradictory finding does not negate the overall pattern in the data.
wrongPassages: Independent replications negate the original result by confirming it in three laboratories.
The amendment was meant to negate the statute by restating its core provisions more clearly.
Further evidence will only negate the theory, which already fits every observation on record.

definition: understood by few; obscure or mysterious
memoryTip: Arcane knowledge sits in a secret arc — only specialists get it.
correctPassage: The paper is full of arcane terminology familiar only to specialists.
wrongPassages: The handbook’s arcane instructions walked first-time users through every step in plain language.
What made the rule arcane was how readily any citizen could recite and apply it.
She preferred arcane explanations that avoided jargon and assumed no prior training.

definition: prevent or hinder progress
memoryTip: Old golf “stymie”: your ball blocks the path — progress is stuck.
correctPassage: Bureaucratic delays continue to stymie efforts to expand the transit line.
wrongPassages: New grants will stymie the lab’s work by removing every remaining bottleneck.
The committee chose to stymie the proposal by voting for it unanimously.
She hoped a quiet afternoon would stymie her focus so the draft would finish early.

definition: essentially different; not alike
memoryTip: Dis-parate: not a matching pair — fundamentally different things.
correctPassage: The report draws on disparate archives that rarely appear in the same study.
wrongPassages: The twins chose disparate outfits that matched down to the last button.
Once every witness agreed, the accounts looked fully disparate.
Editors preferred disparate wording so every chapter sounded the same.

definition: clear of blame; show to be right
memoryTip: Vin-dicate: clear your name — prove you were right all along.
correctPassage: Later measurements helped vindicate the researchers who had challenged the model.
wrongPassages: The new evidence will vindicate the defendant by adding several more charges.
Critics hoped to vindicate her theory by proving every claim was false.
Managers moved to vindicate the report by burying it before the board meeting.

definition: not securely held; dangerously uncertain
memoryTip: So shaky you pray it holds — insecure, chance-dependent.
correctPassage: With only a temporary permit, the clinic’s funding situation remained precarious.
wrongPassages: The steel supports were precarious: inspected, bolted, and rated well above the load.
Her position felt precarious after she received a permanent contract and a raise.
Investors called the surplus precarious because every risk already had a backup plan.

definition: making one feel very happy, excited, or animated
memoryTip: Ex + hilarity — thrills that leave you hilariously alive and buzzing.
correctPassage: For many students, the first independent research breakthrough is exhilarating.
wrongPassages: The three-hour delay on the tarmac was exhilarating for the exhausted passengers.
His exhilarating lecture put half the audience to sleep within minutes.
Parents called the toddler’s long nap exhilarating: quiet, uneventful, and restful.

definition: to bring about or initiate (an action, often trouble)
memoryTip: In-stigate: stir the pot — you start the trouble, not stop it.
correctPassage: Historians still debate which speech did more to instigate the protests that followed.
wrongPassages: The mediator hoped to instigate the dispute by proposing a compromise both sides could accept.
After the audit, managers worked to instigate the errors before the report was published.
She was chosen to instigate the visiting scholar with a careful summary of the research.

definition: having the opposite of the desired effect
memoryTip: Counter + productive: works against the goal, not toward it.
correctPassage: Strict attendance rules proved counterproductive when students began skipping class to avoid penalties.
wrongPassages: The revised study plan was counterproductive, lifting the class average by nearly a full letter grade.
Her measured apology was counterproductive and quickly restored trust among the committee members.
Additional practice sessions were counterproductive, so the team improved more rapidly than expected.

definition: the state of keeping careful watch for danger or difficulty
memoryTip: Think night vigil: staying alert and watchful.
correctPassage: Containing the outbreak required constant vigilance from clinics across the region.
wrongPassages: His vigilance was clear when he dismissed every warning light on the control panel.
They demonstrated vigilance by leaving the laboratory unsecured after the final shift.
