She showed vigilance by skimming the contract once and signing without further review.

definition: in a way that seems self-contradictory yet may be true
memoryTip: Paradox: looks impossible, but still holds — 'oddly, both ways true.'
correctPassage: Paradoxically, lengthening the school day left students less engaged in afternoon classes.
wrongPassages: The experiment proceeded paradoxically, with each measurement matching the predicted value.
She explained the theorem paradoxically, restating each premise in clearer language.
The committee voted paradoxically, approving the measure by a wide and expected margin.

definition: of great importance or historical significance
memoryTip: Of great moment — a huge, history-making event, not a brief moment.
correctPassage: The court's decision was a momentous turn in the debate over voting access.
wrongPassages: Updating the department's filing labels was a momentous reform for the archive staff.
He described the three-minute delay as a momentous interruption to the schedule.
Choosing which binder color to use for notes felt like a momentous decision that morning.

definition: not giving way; firm or inflexible
memoryTip: Won't yield — stays rigid, refuses to bend or compromise.
correctPassage: Negotiators faced an unyielding counterpart who rejected every proposed compromise.
wrongPassages: The unyielding foam cushion compressed easily under the lightest pressure.
Her unyielding stance softened as soon as a better offer appeared.
They praised his unyielding schedule, which he rewrote after each minor conflict.

definition: faultless; of the highest standard
memoryTip: Im-peccable (no sin/fault) — zero flaws, spotless.
correctPassage: The historian's impeccable documentation earned the study wide scholarly trust.
wrongPassages: Reviewers returned his impeccable draft covered in factual corrections.
The laboratory's impeccable samples arrived contaminated and unusable.
They cited her impeccable punctuality after she missed three consecutive meetings.

definition: having become rigid in habit or attitude; set in old ways
memoryTip: Os = bone — attitudes harden like bone, stuck and inflexible.
correctPassage: What began as provisional guidelines had ossified into inflexible doctrine.
wrongPassages: The department's habits ossified into a culture of constant experimentation.
She ossified the mixture by stirring until it became smooth and pourable.
Their ossified platform welcomed frequent policy reversals and fresh initiatives.

definition: to publicly declare something or someone to be wrong or evil
memoryTip: De-nounce: publicly name and call out as wrong.
correctPassage: Several legislators rose to denounce the measure as a threat to civil liberties.
wrongPassages: The governor stepped forward to denounce the volunteers for their outstanding service.
Critics denounce the film as a landmark achievement in documentary storytelling.
She denounced the nomination by accepting the post and praising the selection committee.

definition: to make weak or feeble
memoryTip: De-ability: drain strength until someone can barely function.
correctPassage: Prolonged malnutrition can debilitate patients long after the original illness has passed.
wrongPassages: Coaches designed the regimen to debilitate athletes and leave them stronger for competition.
A week of rest debilitated her so thoroughly that she returned fully restored.
Additional staffing will debilitate the clinic and allow it to serve more patients.

definition: to hinder or impede the progress of
memoryTip: Like a laundry basket in the doorway — blocks the way.
correctPassage: Shortage of trained staff continues to hamper the hospital’s recovery efforts.
wrongPassages: New funding will hamper the project by clearing every logistical delay at once.
The redesigned schedule was meant to hamper production by speeding every stage of assembly.
Critics said the treaty would hamper trade only by removing tariffs and opening new markets.

definition: to appease someone's anger; to soothe or calm
memoryTip: Molli- = soft — soften anger, not harden it.
correctPassage: A sincere apology did more to mollify the committee than any formal rebuttal.
wrongPassages: His sarcastic reply was intended to mollify her by deepening the insult.
Leaders sought to mollify the protesters by announcing harsher penalties and more arrests.
She tried to mollify the audience by raising her voice and refusing every request for compromise.

definition: empty, bleak, and abandoned in appearance; feeling forsaken
memoryTip: De-solate: a lonely, empty stretch with no life in sight.
correctPassage: Winter left the mining camp desolate, with boarded windows and empty streets.
wrongPassages: The desolate plaza filled with vendors and music every weekend afternoon.
Tourists praised the desolate waterfront for its crowded cafés and constant foot traffic.
After the festival, the park felt desolate as families stayed late and lights stayed on.

definition: showing refined taste or careful judgment; selective
memoryTip: Not just bias — a discriminating eye picks quality with care.
correctPassage: A discriminating curator rejected several well-known works that lacked historical depth.
wrongPassages: His discriminating palate approved every cheap blend poured at the tasting without hesitation.
She took a discriminating approach to hiring by accepting the first résumé that arrived.
A discriminating buyer grabs whatever is nearest the shelf and never compares options.

definition: acting quickly and rashly, without careful thought
memoryTip: Rides pure impetus — charges ahead before thinking it through.
correctPassage: An impetuous reply in the press conference undid months of careful negotiation.
wrongPassages: Her impetuous strategy rested on six months of pilot data before any public launch.
The impetuous committee postponed the vote until every risk had been reviewed in writing.
He made an impetuous career change only after listing alternatives and consulting mentors.

definition: having a dislike or distrust of humankind
memoryTip: Mis + anthropos (human) — distrusts or dislikes people in general.
correctPassage: Critics traced the narrator's misanthropic tone to years of betrayal by every institution he had trusted.
wrongPassages: The misanthropic mayor spent weekends greeting constituents and hosting open forums at city hall.
Her misanthropic reputation rested on tireless volunteering and an open door for neighbors in need.
Reviewers praised the novel's misanthropic warmth, especially its faith in ordinary human kindness.

definition: stubbornly uncooperative or resistant to authority
memoryTip: Re-calcitrant: digs in heels and kicks back — won't cooperate.
correctPassage: Even after repeated warnings, the recalcitrant contractor ignored safety protocols and delayed inspections.
wrongPassages: The recalcitrant intern finished every assignment early and asked supervisors for additional work.
Recalcitrant delegates signed the compromise without amendment and thanked the chair for her leadership.
Coaches valued her recalcitrant attitude because she accepted every correction without argument.

definition: lacking a plan or purpose; jumping from thing to thing
memoryTip: De-sultory leaps: hops around with no clear direction.
correctPassage: Their desultory discussion skipped from budgets to parking to cafeteria menus without settling a single vote.
wrongPassages: His desultory outline marched chapter by chapter through each required unit in strict sequence.
The desultory audit followed a fixed checklist and closed every account before moving on.
She delivered a desultory lecture that never left the prepared slides or the stated thesis.

definition: used for emphasis to mean genuine or true; real
memoryTip: Very + true — a genuine thing: a veritable flood of emails.
correctPassage: After the merger, the firm became a veritable archive of industry patents and technical manuals.
wrongPassages: The deserted plaza was a veritable throng of vendors, tourists, and street musicians.
Two mild notices made the play a veritable triumph according to every major critic that week.
She hoped to veritable the rumor by checking three independent sources before publishing.

definition: to faint or nearly faint from extreme emotion
memoryTip: Classic romance trope: so overwhelmed you almost faint.
correctPassage: Audience members seemed ready to swoon as the final aria rose and held a trembling high note.
wrongPassages: She managed to swoon through the dense textbook and still outline every chapter cleanly.
Analysts planned to swoon the quarterly data into a clearer set of regional charts.
The coach urged the team to swoon harder in the final mile if they wanted the medal.

definition: taking effect from a date in the past
memoryTip: Retro = back: the rule reaches backward in time.
correctPassage: The pay raise was retroactive to January, so employees received months of back pay.
wrongPassages: The regulation is strictly retroactive, applying only to conduct that occurs after the law is signed.
Because the scholarship was retroactive, recipients had to wait until next fall before any funds arrived.
The board described its plan as retroactive to emphasize that it would reshape only future hiring.

definition: respond to a gesture or action with a corresponding one
memoryTip: Reciprocal: give back the same kind of gesture you got.
correctPassage: When one nation cut tariffs, trading partners were expected to reciprocate.
wrongPassages: She managed to reciprocate every favor by accepting help while never returning any of her own.
Editors asked him to reciprocate the draft until it was half its original length.
The foundation hoped donors would reciprocate by receiving gifts rather than offering any of their own.

definition: withdraw from involvement; detach
memoryTip: Dis + engage: unhook yourself and step away.
correctPassage: Mediators urged both armies to disengage and pull back from the border.
wrongPassages: The firm moved to disengage three new markets, deepening its presence in each region.
She tried to disengage the audience by lingering on every detail of the opening anecdote.
Regulators will disengage the winning proposal after scoring each submission.

definition: causing or likely to cause argument; quarrelsome
memoryTip: Full of contention — built to start a fight.
correctPassage: Land rights remain a contentious issue that splits the community.
wrongPassages: The report was contentious, offering a calm summary that every faction accepted without debate.
Negotiators preferred the contentious draft because its language left almost no room for dispute.
Reviewers praised her contentious style for smoothing over disagreement and preserving goodwill.

definition: open to more than one interpretation; ambiguous
memoryTip: Equi-vocal: equal voices, so the meaning cuts both ways.
correctPassage: His answer was deliberately equivocal, satisfying neither side completely.
wrongPassages: The statute was carefully equivocal, naming exact thresholds and leaving no interpretive gap.
She delivered an equivocal endorsement, praising the nominee without a single reservation.
Lab results were equivocal in their precision, matching the predicted values to the last decimal.

definition: not clearly visible or attracting attention
memoryTip: In-conspicuous: the opposite of flashy — easy to miss.
correctPassage: The researcher preferred an inconspicuous seat near the exit, where she could observe without drawing notice.
wrongPassages: Her inconspicuous jacket, bright red and covered in reflective logos, drew stares across the plaza.
The museum placed the artifact in an inconspicuous display under a spotlight at the gallery entrance.
He made an inconspicuous entrance by pausing mid-aisle until every head had turned toward him.

definition: combine two things into one, often mistakenly
memoryTip: Con-flate: fuse two ideas into one (sometimes wrongly).
correctPassage: Critics warned not to conflate correlation with causation when interpreting the survey results.
wrongPassages: Historians will conflate the two archives by keeping their catalogs carefully separate.
She tried to conflate the dispute by listing each side’s claims without mixing them together.
Engineers plan to conflate the prototype by stripping it down to a single tested component.

definition: build or form again from parts; restore
memoryTip: Re-constitute: put the pieces back together as a whole.
correctPassage: After the merger collapsed, the firm moved quickly to reconstitute its original research division.
wrongPassages: The committee voted to reconstitute the program by dissolving it and redistributing its budget.
Editors will reconstitute the manuscript by cutting several core chapters without replacement.
Officials chose to reconstitute the damaged bridge by leaving the debris exactly as it fell.

definition: lack of interest, enthusiasm, or concern
memoryTip: A-pathos: no feeling — you simply don’t care.
correctPassage: Voter apathy, more than organized opposition, explained the record-low turnout.
wrongPassages: Her apathy for the campaign showed in late nights, extra revisions, and constant volunteer outreach.
The crowd’s apathy erupted into sustained cheers when the underdog took the lead.
Teachers praised the class’s apathy, noting how eagerly students debated every assigned text.

definition: unchanging over time; unable to be altered
memoryTip: Im-mutable: cannot mutate — locked in place forever.
correctPassage: In the theoretical model, the physical constants are treated as immutable.
wrongPassages: Fashion trends proved immutable, shifting dramatically from one season to the next.
His immutable mood swung from elation to frustration within a single meeting.
They kept an immutable schedule so that meetings could be moved whenever conflicts arose.

definition: better or greater than all others of the same kind
memoryTip: No rival left standing — best of its kind.
correctPassage: The archive remains unrivaled in its coverage of early print culture.
wrongPassages: Reviewers called her method unrivaled, then named three approaches that surpassed it on every measure.
The program’s unrivaled outcomes placed it last among district schools in both retention and test gains.
Investors dismissed the design as unrivaled, meaning it offered nothing distinct from existing products.

definition: come together from different directions toward one point
memoryTip: Con-verge: paths meet at the same spot.
correctPassage: Independent studies continue to converge on the same explanation for the population decline.
wrongPassages: The hikers planned to converge by choosing trails that led them steadily farther apart.
Public opinion will converge only if respondents keep disagreeing on every major issue.
As talks stalled, the negotiators’ positions began to converge into two incompatible camps.

definition: free from a constraint, difficulty, or entanglement
memoryTip: Ex-tricate: pull yourself free from a trap or mess.
correctPassage: Diplomats worked for months to extricate the hostages before winter closed the border.
wrongPassages: She tried to extricate herself by signing new clauses that only tightened the original constraints.
The editor hoped to extricate the draft by weaving in still more conflicting source claims.
Investors moved to extricate the firm by loading it with debt that deepened its obligations.

definition: instruction or guidance under a teacher or guardian
memoryTip: Tutor’s wing: learning under someone’s care and teaching.
correctPassage: Under her tutelage, the young violinist advanced with remarkable speed.
wrongPassages: His years of tutelage meant he had never once received formal instruction or feedback.
The fellowship’s tutelage required scholars to work alone, without mentors or coursework.
She completed her tutelage by refusing every offer of coaching and practicing in isolation.

definition: be an early sign or version of something later
memoryTip: Pre-figure: an early sketch of what is still to come.
correctPassage: Those early sketches already prefigure the building’s final silhouette.
wrongPassages: Historians claimed the treaty prefigured the war only after hostilities had already ended.
The sequel is said to prefigure the original novel by repeating plot points readers already know.
Analysts expect the new data to prefigure past recessions by arriving years after those downturns.

definition: establish so firmly that change becomes difficult
memoryTip: Dig a trench and stay put — hard to dig out later.
correctPassage: Years of unchallenged procedure had entrenched practices that later reforms struggled to reverse.
wrongPassages: The committee hoped to entrench the old policy by discarding it after a single meeting.
Volunteers entrenched the trail by clearing brush so hikers could pass more easily.
She tried to entrench the dough by kneading it lightly and leaving it soft and pliable.

definition: lay down as a rule; authorize a treatment
memoryTip: Pre-scribe: write the rule or medicine ahead of time.
correctPassage: The new protocol prescribes a mandatory cooling-off period before any major budget reallocation.
wrongPassages: The handbook prescribes overtime by forbidding any work beyond the scheduled shift.
Physicians prescribe rest by requiring patients to resume intense training the same day.
The board prescribed the proposal only after refusing to set any rules about how it should proceed.

definition: noticeable in an unwelcome or intrusive way
memoryTip: Ob-trude: sticks out where it doesn’t belong.
correctPassage: An obtrusive watermark across the image distracted readers from the underlying data.
wrongPassages: The observer remained obtrusive by standing well outside the room and never speaking.
Her obtrusive notes were written so lightly that the instructor asked her to rewrite them darker.
Designers praised the obtrusive controls, which stayed hidden until a user actively requested them.

definition: having a mysterious or obscure meaning
memoryTip: Like a cryptogram — meaning locked behind a code.
correctPassage: The footnote was so cryptic that even specialists debated what the author intended.
wrongPassages: Her cryptic directions listed each turn, street name, and landmark in plain sequence.
The diagram was cryptic, with bold labels and a full key explaining every symbol.
He delivered a cryptic summary that left the committee with no ambiguity about next steps.

definition: fill up again; restore a supply
memoryTip: Re-plenish: make full again after something is used up.
correctPassage: After the harvest, farmers used compost and irrigation to replenish nutrients in the soil.
wrongPassages: The editor planned to replenish the manuscript by cutting several supporting sections.
City planners hoped to replenish downtown traffic by closing two of the three main arteries.
She replenished the emergency fund by withdrawing most of its remaining balance.

definition: showy; designed to impress or attract notice
memoryTip: OSTENTatious — put on a show (like a gold tent) so everyone stares.
correctPassage: Critics dismissed the lobby's ostentatious marble staircase as an attempt to advertise success rather than welcome visitors.
wrongPassages: She chose an ostentatious route through side streets so that no one would notice her arrival.
The archive kept the manuscript in an ostentatious vault designed to avoid drawing public attention.
His ostentatious lecture relied on plain language and avoided any flourish that might distract the audience.

definition: based on incomplete information; speculative
memoryTip: Conjecture = a guess — conjectural claims rest on guesswork, not proof.
correctPassage: Historians treated the dynasty's early years as largely conjectural because so few contemporary records survived.
wrongPassages: The lab's conjectural measurements matched the certified reference sample to the last decimal place.
Her conjectural itinerary listed every appointment she had already confirmed in writing.
The prosecution rested on conjectural evidence: fingerprints, surveillance video, and a signed confession.

definition: strict, precise, and exacting
memoryTip: String-tight rules — pulled taut; no slack allowed.
correctPassage: Stringent safety standards apply to every chemical handled in the laboratory.
wrongPassages: The dress code was so stringent that students could arrive in whatever they preferred.
Under the new stringent policy, almost any excuse was accepted without documentation.
Reviewers praised the paper's stringent analysis, which left key terms undefined and methods unexplained.

definition: excessively self-centered or conceited
memoryTip: Ego-tistical: the ego is the star of every sentence.
correctPassage: An egotistical refusal to share credit quickly damaged team morale.
wrongPassages: Her egotistical mentoring always put the interns' growth ahead of her own reputation.
Colleagues admired his egotistical habit of crediting others whenever a project succeeded.
Critics called the memoir egotistical for dwelling almost entirely on other people's achievements.

definition: easily bent; easily influenced
memoryTip: Pliant ≈ pliable — bends without breaking; yields to pressure.
correctPassage: Young stems are pliant enough to train along a trellis without snapping.
wrongPassages: The pliant steel girder held its shape even under the crane's full load.
A pliant negotiator refused every concession no matter how persuasive the counteroffer.
Jurors found the judge pliant: she never bent her ruling once the statute was clear.

definition: calm, peaceful, and untroubled
memoryTip: Serene scene — still water, no wind, no worry.
correctPassage: By midmorning the harbor was serene, its surface unbroken except by a few slow fishing boats.
wrongPassages: The trading floor stayed serene as alarms sounded and brokers shouted over one another.
Her serene reply included slammed binders, interrupted speakers, and a walkout from the panel.
Reviewers called the finale serene for its frantic pacing and unresolved arguments among the cast.

definition: experienced through another person rather than firsthand
memoryTip: Via someone else — you feel their thrills secondhand.
correctPassage: Many readers find a vicarious thrill in the explorer's journals without ever leaving home.
wrongPassages: She earned a vicarious diploma by attending every seminar and sitting every exam in person.
His vicarious injury resulted from the fall he took on the ice during practice.
They booked a vicarious itinerary under their own names and flew out the following week.

definition: prevent or hinder by taking action ahead of time
memoryTip: Fore-stall: block it before it starts.
correctPassage: Public-health officials hoped early testing would forestall a wider outbreak in the region.
wrongPassages: They moved to forestall the leak only after the basement had already filled with water.
Management forestalled the shortfall by ignoring the first dozen budget warnings.
She forestalled the deadline by delivering the report three weeks after it was due.

definition: diminish or shrink gradually
memoryTip: Dwindle down — shrink little by little until almost gone.
correctPassage: As grant funding dwindled, the lab had to close two of its three field stations.
wrongPassages: Enrollment dwindled from forty students to several hundred within a single term.
The surplus dwindled after three consecutive quarters of record profits and expansion.
Her confidence dwindled into a keynote that packed the largest auditorium on campus.

definition: tending to provoke a strong reaction, interest, or annoyance
memoryTip: Pro-voke: built to stir a reaction, not to soothe.
correctPassage: The historian's provocative thesis challenged long-accepted accounts of the treaty talks.
wrongPassages: The workshop was so provocative that participants left calm, unchallenged, and ready for sleep.
His provocative apology settled every dispute and left no one unsettled or curious.
Students called the review sheet provocative because it restated only the simplest drills.

definition: the state of being dormant or delayed until conditions allow activity
memoryTip: Latent stage — hidden or idle until something triggers it.
correctPassage: Epidemiologists measured a latency of several weeks between exposure and the first detectable symptoms.
wrongPassages: The system showed no latency: every command executed the moment it was issued.
Her latency at the podium meant she began speaking before the chair finished the introduction.
The volcano’s latency produced continuous eruptions that never paused long enough for ash to settle.

definition: develop slowly under favorable conditions; keep warm to hatch or grow
memoryTip: Like eggs in an incubator — grow slowly under steady care.
correctPassage: The research group planned to incubate promising prototypes in a low-pressure pilot program before scaling production.
wrongPassages: Editors decided to incubate the unfinished draft by publishing it on the front page the same afternoon.
Managers hoped to incubate the fragile partnership by cutting all joint funding overnight.
She incubated the seedlings by leaving them outdoors during the first hard freeze of the season.

definition: combined effect greater than the sum of the parts
memoryTip: Syn + energy: working together multiplies the power.
correctPassage: Analysts argued that synergy between the design and manufacturing teams would cut costs without lowering quality.
wrongPassages: Working in isolation, she produced more synergy than any of the collaborative projects on the calendar.
The departments claimed synergy while rejecting every proposal that required them to share resources.
Rival firms created synergy by refusing to coordinate and by undercutting each other’s bids.

definition: wary and careful; unwilling to take unnecessary risks
memoryTip: Circum-spect: look all around before you step.
correctPassage: Counsel urged a circumspect public statement until the investigation clarified the remaining facts.
wrongPassages: His circumspect dive off the pier disregarded every posted warning about submerged rocks.
A circumspect investor shifted the entire portfolio into a single unvetted tip the day it appeared.
She offered a circumspect reply that promised sweeping reforms before any review had begun.

definition: innocent and without deception
memoryTip: Without guile (tricks) — open, honest, nothing up the sleeve.
correctPassage: The witness’s guileless account matched the documents and left little room for doubt about the timeline.
wrongPassages: The guileless negotiator hid two conflicting offers and revealed each only when it served her side.
His guileless pitch omitted the fees that would appear only after customers signed the contract.
A guileless broker rearranged account labels so clients could not see where the funds had gone.

definition: pacify someone by giving in to demands
memoryTip: A-peace: buy quiet by yielding a little (or a lot).
correctPassage: Officials hoped a modest concession would appease critics without rewriting the entire policy.
wrongPassages: The mayor sought to appease residents by rejecting every petition they had filed.
She tried to appease the client by escalating the dispute into a public lawsuit.
The firm hoped to appease regulators by concealing the audit findings entirely.

definition: teach someone to accept a set of beliefs uncritically
memoryTip: In-doctrine: pour in a doctrine; no free questioning allowed.
correctPassage: Critics claimed the program sought to indoctrinate recruits rather than encourage independent judgment.
wrongPassages: The seminar was designed to indoctrinate students by requiring them to challenge every claim.
She hoped to indoctrinate the class through open debate and competing primary sources.
The lab manual aimed to indoctrinate curiosity, not loyalty to a single fixed theory.

definition: new and experimental, especially in the arts
memoryTip: French for "vanguard" — out front of the artistic pack.
correctPassage: The festival championed avant-garde compositions that abandoned conventional melody and form.
wrongPassages: The museum's avant-garde wing featured only the most conservative nineteenth-century portraits.
Editors called the report avant-garde because it followed the agency's standard template exactly.
His avant-garde lecture restated the textbook definitions without offering a single new claim.

definition: intellectual rather than emotional or physical
memoryTip: Cerebrum = brain — more thinking than feeling.
correctPassage: The documentary is deliberately cerebral, favoring close analysis over spectacle or sentiment.
wrongPassages: Reviewers called the chase sequence cerebral for its nonstop crashes and almost no dialogue.
Fans praised the cerebral finale for its tearful reunions and total silence on ideas.
Coaches designed a cerebral drill that tested only sprint speed and vertical jump.

definition: persuade by flattery or gentle urging
memoryTip: Cage + jolly talk — sweet-talk someone into the cage (or the favor).
correctPassage: She managed to cajole several reluctant donors into covering the shortfall with well-timed praise.
wrongPassages: He tried to cajole the clerk by pounding the desk and threatening to call security.
They cajoled the committee with a cold memo and no attempt at personal persuasion.
The general hoped to cajole the city by imposing a curfew and cutting off supplies.

definition: easily shaped or influenced; pliable
memoryTip: Hit metal with a mallet—malleable stuff bends; minds can bend too.
correctPassage: Public opinion on the referendum remained malleable until the final week of campaigning.
wrongPassages: The bylaws proved so malleable that no amendment could alter them for decades.
Her malleable stance never shifted, even when new evidence challenged her assumptions.
Engineers prized the malleable beam because it refused to bend under any load.

definition: well chosen or suited to the circumstances
memoryTip: Felicity = apt happiness—a felicitous phrase is a happily perfect fit.
correctPassage: The speaker's felicitous analogy clarified a dense economic concept for the audience.
wrongPassages: Critics called the title felicitous because it misled readers about the book's actual subject.
His felicitous remark derailed the negotiation and left both parties offended.
They selected a felicitous venue only after confirming it lacked every amenity the conference required.

definition: extreme care and attention to detail
memoryTip: Meticulous = tiny details—meticulousness is extreme care, not speed.
correctPassage: The archivist's meticulousness preserved fragile manuscripts that lesser care would have damaged.
wrongPassages: His meticulousness showed in the rushed draft, which skipped citations and left figures unlabeled.
The lab's meticulousness meant measurements were taken once and never double-checked.
Reviewers praised her meticulousness for a report that ignored half the required sections.

definition: give strength or energy to
memoryTip: In + vigor: put vigor in—energize, wake up, strengthen.
correctPassage: A change of leadership can invigorate an organization that has grown stagnant.
wrongPassages: The endless briefing seemed to invigorate staff, who left more exhausted than when they arrived.
Budget cuts were meant to invigorate the program by eliminating training and travel support.
Physicians warned that sleepless nights would invigorate patients recovering from surgery.

definition: in original condition; unspoiled
memoryTip: Priest-clean pure—pristine means untouched, unspoiled original condition.
correctPassage: Researchers sought a pristine stretch of forest where human activity had left little trace.
wrongPassages: After decades of mining runoff, the lake remained pristine with cloudy water and sparse fish.
The gallery described the canvas as pristine despite deep scratches and a torn corner.
His pristine notes were smudged, incomplete, and missing several required diagrams.

definition: detract from; disparage
memoryTip: De-rogate: take rank away—derogate means diminish or speak down of.
correctPassage: Nothing in the agreement should derogate from existing labor rights.
wrongPassages: The keynote was crafted to derogate the scientist for her careful, widely cited research.
Conservators hoped to derogate the damaged fresco by restoring its original colors.
Alumni rose to derogate the retiring dean with tributes and a standing ovation.

definition: regard with great respect
memoryTip: Venus-level reverence—venerate means treat as sacred or deeply respect.
correctPassage: Many still venerate the founders while questioning later policy choices.
wrongPassages: The editorial chose to venerate the official with a scathing indictment of his record.
She hoped a terse apology would venerate the insult and erase its public impact.
Critics venerate a novel when they dismiss it as careless, dull, and forgettable.

definition: cheerful and not serious
memoryTip: Light heart—cheerful, playful, not heavy or grim.
correctPassage: A light-hearted tone made the difficult subject easier to discuss.
wrongPassages: The light-hearted eulogy left the family shaken with its stark account of loss.
Her light-hearted brief demanded substantial damages and a multi-year injunction.
The light-hearted safety chapter listed only the most severe injury protocols.

definition: cause to happen suddenly; acting rashly
memoryTip: Like rain precipitating—things fall fast; a precipitate act is rash.
correctPassage: A sudden price spike can precipitate panic selling.
wrongPassages: The board’s precipitate review stretched over five years of deliberate study.
Negotiators hoped to precipitate calm by postponing any decision for several months.
A precipitate strategy is one that waits until every risk has been fully eliminated.

definition: examine closely and thoroughly
memoryTip: Scrutiny = close look—scrutinize means study every detail carefully.
correctPassage: Peer reviewers will scrutinize every claim before the paper is accepted.
wrongPassages: Editors claimed to scrutinize the manuscript after skimming only the abstract.
She scrutinized the contract for a few seconds and signed without reading further.
To scrutinize the budget, the committee approved it without opening a single page.

definition: having mixed or conflicting feelings
memoryTip: Ambi = both ways—ambivalent means pulled in two directions at once.
correctPassage: She remained ambivalent about the offer, drawn by the salary yet wary of the longer commute.
wrongPassages: The committee was ambivalent: every member cast a firm, identical vote of approval.
His ambivalent endorsement left no doubt that he fully backed the proposal.
Ambivalent about the outcome, she felt only pure excitement with no second thoughts.

definition: based on or involving analogy
memoryTip: Analogy = comparison—analogical reasoning maps one case onto another.
correctPassage: Her analogical argument compared the immune system to a well-trained security force.
wrongPassages: The report was purely analogical, listing only raw measurements with no comparisons drawn.
They preferred an analogical method that avoided all metaphor and treated each case in isolation.
An analogical proof, in their view, was one that relied solely on direct observation of the specimen itself.

definition: cause two or more things to change places
memoryTip: Trans-pose: switch places—or move a melody into another key.
correctPassage: The editor asked her to transpose the two paragraphs so the conclusion would come last.
wrongPassages: To transpose the files, she left each document in its original folder untouched.
They hoped to transpose the dispute by ignoring it until interest faded on its own.
The clerk will transpose the inventory by adding new items without rearranging any labels.

definition: the quality of being open and honest
memoryTip: Candid camera honesty—candor is frank, open speech without sugarcoating.
correctPassage: The director's candor about budget shortfalls surprised staff who expected a polished spin.
wrongPassages: His candor consisted of carefully avoiding every difficult question in the interview.
She was praised for candor after delivering only vague, noncommittal answers.
The report's candor lay in its elaborate euphemisms that concealed the real losses.

definition: careful good judgment; caution
memoryTip: Prudent choices—prudence is careful good sense, not reckless risk.
correctPassage: Fiscal prudence led the board to delay expansion until reserves were rebuilt.
wrongPassages: Spending the emergency fund on a speculative venture showed remarkable prudence.
Her prudence was clear when she dismissed every warning and signed without reading.
They celebrated his prudence after he took the largest, least-informed risk of the year.

definition: fair and impartial
memoryTip: Equity = fairness—equitable means just and even-handed to all sides.
correctPassage: The board sought an equitable settlement that weighed each party's claims without favoring the strongest.
wrongPassages: Critics called the plan equitable because it funneled nearly all benefits to a single stakeholder.
An equitable hearing, as they defined it, meant deciding the case before the weaker side spoke.
She praised the equitable contract for locking minority partners out of any real influence.

definition: not able to be reached or achieved
memoryTip: Can't attain it—unattainable means out of reach, not merely hard.
correctPassage: For many applicants, admission to the program remains unattainable without substantial financial aid.
wrongPassages: The once unattainable target was finished before lunch on the team's first quiet day.
Hikers called the ridge unattainable only after the new trail delivered them to the summit.
She treated the unattainable deadline as generous, since the report had already been submitted.

definition: offering nothing stimulating; bland
memoryTip: Vapor-thin flavor—vapid talk is bland, empty, and quickly forgotten.
correctPassage: Though polished in delivery, the keynote remained vapid, offering little beyond familiar slogans.
wrongPassages: Reviewers called the seminar vapid for packing each hour with dense analysis and sharp examples.
The vapid novel kept readers awake with twists that unsettled every assumption they held.
Students preferred the vapid lectures because the arguments forced them to rethink their positions.

definition: a penalty for disobeying; or official permission
memoryTip: Two-faced word: sanctions punish—or sanction means officially allow.
correctPassage: The league may sanction the franchise for repeated violations of recruitment rules.
wrongPassages: Officials moved to sanction the misconduct by promoting those responsible and expanding their budget.
She claimed she could sanction the treaty simply by forgetting to schedule any formal review.
The committee hoped to sanction the reform by refusing to put it on the agenda at all.

definition: the state of being out of place or inconsistent
memoryTip: Incongruous mismatch—incongruity is when pieces simply don't fit.
correctPassage: Critics noted a striking incongruity between the company's green pledges and its rising emissions.
wrongPassages: The matching set showed perfect incongruity: every piece shared the same color, scale, and style.
Historians praised the incongruity of the two accounts, which agreed on every material detail.
Reviewers welcomed the incongruity of the argument, as each claim reinforced the next without tension.

definition: combine or unite into one
memoryTip: Dental amalgam mixes metals — amalgamate = blend into one.
correctPassage: The two small clinics will amalgamate next year into a single regional center.
wrongPassages: The board voted to amalgamate the joint venture by splitting it into three independent firms.
Editors hoped to amalgamate the essay by removing every cross-reference that linked its sections.
Planners amalgamated downtown traffic by closing the connecting bridges between the districts.

definition: formally announce or make widely known
memoryTip: Pro-mulgate: put the rule out so everyone hears it.
correctPassage: The agency will promulgate the new safety standards before the compliance deadline.
wrongPassages: Officials sought to promulgate the findings by sealing the report and limiting access to counsel.
She promulgated the policy change only after ensuring no employee would ever hear of it.
The committee promulgated the revised guidelines by withdrawing them from the public record.

definition: mutual exchange for mutual benefit
memoryTip: Reciprocal: you give, I give back — mutual benefit.
correctPassage: Trade negotiators insisted on reciprocity so each country would open its markets equally.
wrongPassages: Under a policy of reciprocity, only one side ever paid while the other kept taking.
The alliance practiced reciprocity by accepting every favor and never returning any.
Critics praised the treaty’s reciprocity clause because obligations flowed in one direction only.

definition: involve as a necessary consequence
memoryTip: En-tail: the decision drags consequences along behind it.
correctPassage: Accepting the fellowship will entail relocating for at least two years.
wrongPassages: The promotion will entail no new duties, oversight, or changes to her current schedule.
Reviewers argued that the reform entailed success only if every required step were optional.
Expanding the study will entail dropping the control group and ignoring follow-up data.

definition: demand or specify as a condition of an agreement
memoryTip: Stipulate the terms — spell out conditions in the deal.
correctPassage: The contract stipulates that all research data remain public for five years.
wrongPassages: Counsel refused to stipulate any terms, leaving the settlement entirely open-ended.
The landlord stipulated rent by never naming a figure or writing one into the lease.
Negotiators stipulated confidentiality only after stripping the deal of every stated condition.

definition: serving as a symbol of something
memoryTip: Like an emblem — stands for a bigger idea or era.
correctPassage: The abandoned mill became emblematic of the town's industrial decline.
wrongPassages: Traders sought emblematic prices that never rose or fell more than a fraction of a percent.
The empty appendix was emblematic of a report dense with charts, tables, and findings.
Her thoroughly ordinary lunch order was somehow emblematic of radical culinary innovation.

definition: a reduction or lessening
memoryTip: A-bate: turn down the volume — reduction (noise abatement).
correctPassage: Noise abatement measures cut late-night complaints from nearby residents.
wrongPassages: After the abatement of the storm, winds grew stronger and flooding spread downtown.
The board celebrated the abatement of sales when quarterly revenue hit a record high.
With no abatement of the fever, her temperature finally returned to normal overnight.

definition: lack of harmony; clash of sounds or ideas
memoryTip: Dis-sonance: harsh sound or clash — ideas that don't fit.
correctPassage: Voters sensed dissonance between the campaign's promises and its budget plan.
wrongPassages: The choir's seamless unison was praised as pure dissonance from the opening bar.
Panelists showed striking dissonance: each restated the same conclusion without objection.
Critics admired the essay's dissonance, noting how every paragraph reinforced one thesis.

definition: reduce in extent or cut short
memoryTip: Cut the tail short — reduce or trim back.
correctPassage: Budget cuts will curtail after-school programs for the rest of the year.
wrongPassages: The firm curtailed production by running every plant at full capacity around the clock.
To curtail the ceremony, organizers added two hours of speeches and musical numbers.
New funding will curtail the library's hours by keeping branches open later each night.

definition: courage and strength in pain or adversity
memoryTip: Fort + attitude — inner strength when things get hard.
correctPassage: Survivors showed remarkable fortitude during the long months of recovery.
wrongPassages: He displayed fortitude by abandoning the project at the first minor setback.
Her fortitude consisted of avoiding every difficult assignment offered that semester.
Under pressure, his fortitude showed mainly as panic whenever a problem appeared.

definition: serious, strict, and unrelenting
memoryTip: A stern face — no jokes, strict and unyielding.
correctPassage: The principal’s stern reprimand made clear that further absences would not be excused.
wrongPassages: His stern grin and joking asides put the nervous applicants completely at ease.
The guidelines’ stern flexibility invited each department to invent its own standards.
Critics praised the novel’s stern digressions, which wandered freely from any central plot.

definition: accurately predicting what will happen
memoryTip: Like a prophet — foresaw what later came true.
correctPassage: Her early essay now seems prophetic in light of the reforms that followed.
wrongPassages: His prophetic forecast failed to anticipate any of the market’s subsequent swings.
Editors called the revised budget prophetic because it merely restated last year’s figures.
A prophetic footnote listed sources the author had already cited in the main text.

definition: publicly denounce or condemn
memoryTip: De-cry: cry out against something in public.
correctPassage: Local historians decry the demolition of the century-old theater.
wrongPassages: Reviewers decried the film by awarding it top prizes and urging a wider release.
She decried the renovation plan by volunteering to oversee construction herself.
Donors decried the museum’s new wing with a multiyear grant and a gala opening.

definition: lack of seriousness; disrespectful levity
memoryTip: Flip answers — unserious jokes when gravity is needed.
correctPassage: Flippancy about lab safety rules has no place during hazardous experiments.
wrongPassages: Her flippancy showed in the careful, solemn tone she used throughout the eulogy.
The judge praised the witness’s flippancy for treating each question with full gravity.
Protocol required flippancy from every speaker, so each address remained formal and restrained.

definition: having peculiar or unexpected traits
memoryTip: Full of quirks — oddly charming little peculiarities.
correctPassage: The café’s quirky menu pairs familiar dishes with unexpected spice blends.
wrongPassages: The completely standard office layout was praised as quirky for matching every other floor.
His quirky schedule never varied by a minute across ten identical workdays.
Analysts called the forecast quirky because it rested on conventional assumptions alone.

definition: courtesy and mutual respect among people or nations
memoryTip: Comity ≈ committee of courtesy — polite mutual respect.
correctPassage: Years of diplomatic comity made the trade negotiations unusually free of public recrimination.
wrongPassages: The sudden collapse of comity between the two ministries was celebrated as a triumph of open hostility.
Critics praised the firm’s comity when it refused every request for cooperation from its rivals.
Historians attributed the alliance’s success to comity that required neither courtesy nor mutual restraint.

definition: bitingly sharp or critically caustic
memoryTip: Mord- = bite — mordant wit has a sharp bite.
correctPassage: The essay’s mordant asides undercut the official narrative without ever raising its voice.
wrongPassages: Her mordant tribute was so gentle that even the subject’s fiercest critics found nothing sharp in it.
The committee issued a mordant report that carefully avoided any note of criticism or irony.
Students welcomed the instructor’s mordant feedback, which consisted only of mild encouragement.

definition: involving a heavy burden or obligation
memoryTip: Onus = burden — an onerous task is crushingly heavy.
correctPassage: Compliance with the new audit rules proved onerous for clinics already short of administrative staff.
wrongPassages: Applicants found the one-page form so onerous that most finished it in under a minute.
The board described the unpaid internship as onerous precisely because it demanded almost no work.
Reformers called the regulations onerous for removing every significant obligation on large firms.

definition: a false appearance; a claim not based in fact
memoryTip: Pretend-sense — a fake show of something real.
correctPassage: Under the pretense of a routine inspection, investigators gathered evidence for weeks.
wrongPassages: The witness’s pretense of the timeline was later confirmed by three independent cameras.
Researchers trusted the paper’s pretense because every claim matched the published data set.
With full pretense, the auditor listed every conflict of interest in the public record.

definition: given to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood or behavior
memoryTip: Like a goat’s caper — sudden leaps of mood or decision.
correctPassage: Capricious grading left students unable to predict which criteria would matter from week to week.
wrongPassages: The agency’s capricious schedule never varied, repeating the same sequence every quarter.
Investors preferred the fund’s capricious strategy because it followed a fixed formula for decades.
Her capricious habits—rising at six, reviewing the same checklist—made each day identical to the last.

definition: delay or prevent something bad from happening
memoryTip: Hold off danger with a stave (staff) — keep the bad thing at bay.
correctPassage: Emergency subsidies helped the district stave off mass teacher layoffs through the budget shortfall.
wrongPassages: Negotiators hoped to stave off the agreement by signing the treaty the same afternoon.
The early diagnosis staved off recovery by letting the infection spread untreated for weeks.
City planners staved off congestion by adding more cars to the already crowded routes.

definition: make happen sooner or more quickly
memoryTip: Think expedition: speed the process so it arrives sooner.
correctPassage: The agency agreed to expedite review of the permit so construction could begin before winter.
wrongPassages: Editors expedited the article by holding it for three extra rounds of revision.
Shipping clerks expedited the package by placing it at the bottom of the outbound queue.
The board expedited the vote by postponing discussion until the following fiscal year.

definition: rate at which people leave and are replaced; or total sales
memoryTip: Staff or stock turns over — how fast people/goods cycle through.
correctPassage: High staff turnover forced the clinic to retrain new nurses every few months.
wrongPassages: Managers celebrated the department's turnover after almost no one resigned in five years.
Retail analysts praised the store's turnover when weekly sales fell to their lowest point.
Investors fretted over staff turnover after every senior researcher stayed through the decade.

definition: restrain or suppress
memoryTip: Stifle a yawn or a fire — smother it so it cannot break free.
correctPassage: Heavy censorship can stifle public debate long before any formal ban is announced.
wrongPassages: Open forums were designed to stifle dissent by giving every critic an equal turn to speak.
The scholarship fund stifled talent by removing financial barriers for promising applicants.
Engineers stifled the alarm so the siren would sound louder across the facility.

definition: withdraw a former statement or belief
memoryTip: Re-cant: sing the claim again the other way — take it back.
correctPassage: Under cross-examination, the expert recanted the claim she had made in her initial report.
wrongPassages: The senator recanted her earlier criticism by repeating the same attack in a second speech.
After reviewing the data, the authors recanted their hypothesis by restating it without change.
He recanted the apology by adding further details that made his original admission stronger.

definition: easy to control, manage, or influence
memoryTip: Tractable like a tract you can handle — easy to manage or solve.
correctPassage: Once the variables were reduced, the optimization problem became tractable for the research team.
wrongPassages: The software was so tractable that technicians could not adjust a single parameter.
Negotiators abandoned the plan after finding the opposing side unexpectedly tractable and unwilling to compromise.
A tractable dispute is one that has resisted every mediation attempt for decades.

definition: full of danger or risk
memoryTip: Packed with peril — clearly dangerous.
correctPassage: Crossing the ridge in a winter storm would be perilous even for experienced climbers.
wrongPassages: The committee described the fully insured, low-stakes pilot program as perilous for the district.
A perilous commute meant empty roads and uninterrupted green lights the entire way home.
Inspectors labeled the newly reinforced bridge perilous because every support had been tested twice.

definition: irritate intensely; infuriate
memoryTip: Ex-asperate: push past the last of someone's patience.
correctPassage: Repeated billing errors began to exasperate clients who had already waited weeks for a correction.
wrongPassages: The nurse hoped to exasperate the patient's discomfort with a carefully adjusted dose.
Soft lighting and unhurried service exasperated the spa guests into deep relaxation.
She exasperated the deadline by submitting the report two days ahead of schedule.

definition: speak or write about someone in an abusively critical way
memoryTip: Turn someone into a villain with harsh, smearing words.
correctPassage: Opponents tried to vilify the researcher rather than engage the evidence she presented.
wrongPassages: The host planned to vilify the guest by recounting only the most impressive achievements of her career.
Editors vilified the manuscript by inserting a few minor grammar corrections and nothing more.
Donors vilified the foundation by praising its transparency in every public statement.

definition: in agreement or harmony; matching
memoryTip: Like congruent triangles — same shape, in agreement.
correctPassage: Her daily decisions were congruent with the ethical standards she urged her students to follow.
wrongPassages: The two survey maps were congruent in that no boundary on either map aligned with the other.
His public remarks were congruent with his private views only in that they flatly contradicted them.
The committee found the proposal congruent with its goals after rejecting every principle the plan claimed to serve.

definition: fruitfulness; capacity to produce abundantly
memoryTip: Fecund means fertile — fecundity is productive abundance.
correctPassage: Biologists attributed the valley’s harvests to the soil’s unusual fecundity.
wrongPassages: Ecologists cited the desert’s fecundity as the reason almost nothing could grow there.
Critics blamed the studio’s fecundity when years passed without a single finished film.
The speech’s fecundity was plain: nearly half an hour of empty phrases and no substance.

definition: the quality of being diverse in character or content
memoryTip: Hetero = different; heterogeneity is mixed variety.
correctPassage: The city’s cultural heterogeneity is visible in its markets, languages, and festivals.
wrongPassages: Managers prized the product line’s heterogeneity: every unit matched the others exactly.
Genetic heterogeneity was confirmed once every sample proved identical to the control.
The panel’s heterogeneity of views produced a unanimous vote with no dissent recorded.

definition: disperse or scatter; waste or squander
memoryTip: Like mist burning off — scatter away, or waste until nothing remains.
correctPassage: By midday the morning mist had begun to dissipate over the fields.
wrongPassages: Engineers designed the vents to dissipate heat by trapping warm air in a sealed chamber.
Her savings will dissipate if left untouched in a high-interest account for years.
Police tried to dissipate the crowd by directing still more people into the square.

definition: convenience or advantage, often at the expense of principle
memoryTip: What is expedient: the convenient shortcut, not always the right path.
correctPassage: They chose silence out of political expediency rather than conviction.
wrongPassages: Political expediency drove him to reject every shortcut and follow principle alone.
She acted from pure expediency when she took the slower path that preserved her integrity.
The reform succeeded through expediency: years of open debate with no regard for convenience.

definition: the quality of not being precisely fixed or decided
memoryTip: In-determine: not yet fixed — outcome still open.
correctPassage: Legal indeterminacy in the statute left judges wide room to interpret.
wrongPassages: The contract’s indeterminacy listed every price, date, and obligation without ambiguity.
After months of debate, the board praised the plan’s indeterminacy: each step was fixed in writing.
Cartographers valued the map’s indeterminacy for marking every trail to the nearest meter.

definition: ordinary and unexciting; of the everyday world
memoryTip: From monde (world) — plain earthly, everyday stuff.
correctPassage: Between breakthroughs, researchers still handle mundane paperwork and routine correspondence.
wrongPassages: Critics called the premiere mundane for its unprecedented staging and daring score.
Her mundane itinerary included polar expeditions, summit meetings, and rare archival discoveries.
The museum reserved its most mundane gallery for the once-in-a-century loan of royal jewels.

definition: reduction of costs or spending; a pulling back
memoryTip: Re-trench: dig in and cut back spending.
correctPassage: After the boom, corporate retrenchment meant hiring freezes and smaller offices.
wrongPassages: The board framed its retrenchment as a plan to double the payroll and open three new campuses.
Investors cheered the firm's retrenchment into overseas markets it had never entered before.
Festival organizers announced a retrenchment that lengthened hours and added twice as many stages.

definition: be full of or swarming with
memoryTip: Teeming with life — crowded and swarming.
correctPassage: After the rains, the garden paths teem with frogs and insects.
wrongPassages: By midwinter the wetlands teem with silence, empty of birds for miles.
Historians note that the frontier once teemed with vacancy until settlers finally arrived.
After curfew the plaza teems with absence, every stall shuttered and every bench unused.

definition: stir up; make cloudy or agitated
memoryTip: Roil the water — churn mud and feelings into a mess.
correctPassage: Rumors of a merger continue to roil the company's stock price.
wrongPassages: Soft music was intended to roil the waiting room into a calmer, quieter mood.
The mediator hoped to roil the dispute by seating both sides at one table and easing tensions.
Clear water and still conditions allowed divers to roil the pond without clouding a single reading.

definition: involving immoral, dishonorable, or dirty dealings
memoryTip: Sordid like moral dirt — grubby, shameful business.
correctPassage: Reporters exposed the sordid scheme of bribes behind the contract awards.
wrongPassages: Neighbors called the charity drive sordid for raising record funds with full public accounting.
Her sordid reputation rested on decades of transparent, ethical leadership.
Judges praised the witness for a sordid account that matched every document without omission.

definition: unable to be appeased or calmed; relentless
memoryTip: Im-placable: cannot be placated — nothing soothes that anger.
correctPassage: Despite months of talks, the opposition remained implacable and rejected every compromise on the bill.
wrongPassages: A single apology left her implacable, and the quarrel was forgotten by evening.
The committee's implacable agenda left plenty of room for last-minute revisions.
His implacable tone reassured the staff that the criticism would be mild.

definition: harmful or hostile; unfriendly
memoryTip: Enemy-ical — like an enemy: harmful or unfriendly.
correctPassage: Prolonged drought created conditions inimical to the region’s remaining wetlands.
wrongPassages: The mentor’s inimical guidance helped several interns secure permanent positions.
Residents praised the park’s inimical design for making evening walks feel safer.
Mild winters proved inimical to the citrus groves that thrived under frost-free skies.

definition: attribute a quality or fault to someone
memoryTip: Im-pute: put the blame (or a quality) onto someone.
correctPassage: Historians hesitate to impute deliberate deceit when the surviving records are incomplete.
wrongPassages: The analyst hoped to impute the missing figures by re-running the spreadsheet.
She tried to impute the error so that no one on the team would be blamed.
Before the vote, the clerk will impute each ballot into the counting machine.

definition: holding firmly; persistent
memoryTip: Tenax = holding tight — a grip that will not let go.
correctPassage: Tenacious reporting over several years finally exposed how the funds had been diverted.
wrongPassages: His tenacious interest in the topic faded after the opening lecture.
With a tenacious shrug, she abandoned the draft and left the office early.
The coalition’s tenacious support dissolved as soon as the first setback appeared.

definition: producing a beneficial effect
memoryTip: Salute to health — good for you, even when the lesson is harsh.
correctPassage: The audit’s findings had a salutary effect, prompting tighter controls on discretionary spending.
wrongPassages: Skipping every practice session had a salutary effect on her race times.
Critics called the budget cuts salutary only because the services they funded disappeared.
The leak left a salutary stain that spread through the ceiling overnight.

definition: giving a false or misleading impression
memoryTip: Delusion-ive — creates a false belief that feels true.
correctPassage: Investors soon found the promise of risk-free returns delusive once the market corrected.
wrongPassages: The laboratory's delusive instruments matched every certified standard without a single error.
Her delusive summary listed each finding exactly as the peer reviewers had confirmed it.
Analysts praised the delusive forecast for predicting employment gains with unusual accuracy.

definition: full of twists and turns; overly complex
memoryTip: A tortured path — winding twists, or an argument that never ends.
correctPassage: Negotiators spent months on a tortuous route through conflicting statutes before reaching a draft.
wrongPassages: The highway ran in a tortuous straight line across the plain with no curves for miles.
Her tortuous brief reduced the entire dispute to three plain sentences anyone could follow.
He preferred the tortuous staircase that climbed in one unbroken flight to the landing.

definition: attempting to avoid notice; secretive
memoryTip: Fur-tive like a thief's quiet sneak — a secretive glance.
correctPassage: During the hearing he cast a furtive glance at his notes when the chair turned away.
wrongPassages: Her furtive announcement filled the auditorium after days of open press briefings.
The band made a furtive entrance under fireworks while the crowd chanted their names.
He delivered a furtive keynote from the main stage under the hall's brightest spotlights.

definition: expose the falseness of a claim or idea
memoryTip: De-bunk: knock the bunk (nonsense) out — prove it false.
correctPassage: The study aims to debunk popular myths about multitasking and long-term memory.
wrongPassages: Editors moved to debunk the rumor by reprinting it as confirmed fact on the front page.
She hoped to debunk the theory by gathering still more evidence in its favor.
The panel will debunk the proposal by endorsing every claim without further scrutiny.

definition: a distinctive feature or sign of quality
memoryTip: Gold hallmark stamp — the distinctive mark of real quality.
correctPassage: Precision remains the hallmark of her laboratory's published work.
wrongPassages: Confusion is the hallmark of her carefully organized and cross-checked field notes.
Critics called silence the hallmark of the arena during the championship's loudest roar.
Random typos became the hallmark of a manuscript that had passed three rounds of proofreading.

definition: able to be exchanged without changing the result
memoryTip: Inter-change — swap them and nothing really changes.
correctPassage: Because the two reagents proved interchangeable, technicians could substitute either without altering the reaction's outcome.
wrongPassages: The curator called the one-of-a-kind sculpture interchangeable, insisting that no other work could ever take its place.
Investigators labeled her distinctive signature interchangeable with every other mark in the crowded file.
Once each part was sealed and serialized, the engineer declared the components interchangeable only with themselves.

definition: express the essential features of something briefly
memoryTip: In a capsule — sum up the essence in a tight package.
correctPassage: The abstract manages to encapsulate a decade of fieldwork in a single dense paragraph.
wrongPassages: She tried to encapsulate the report by expanding every section with long digressions and asides.
He encapsulated the theory by omitting its central claims and listing only minor footnotes.
The committee encapsulated the crisis by refusing to summarize it and demanding the full archive uncut.

definition: treating a serious matter with deliberate, often inappropriate humor
memoryTip: Facet + joking face — treating serious things lightly on purpose.
correctPassage: A facetious remark during the memorial briefing was widely misread as official policy.
wrongPassages: Her facetious eulogy never once broke into a smile, a joke, or any touch of levity.
The surgeon kept a facetious silence while explaining each clinical risk in careful, humorless detail.
He filed a facetious tax return that listed every income source without a trace of irony.

definition: hidden from view; private and not often visited
memoryTip: Se-clude: shut away — private and hard to reach.
correctPassage: The research cabin sits in a secluded valley reachable only by a rough footpath.
wrongPassages: The secluded plaza hosted a weekend street fair with food trucks and constant crowds.
Her secluded desk stood under bright lights in the center of the open office.
They chose a secluded table next to the host stand at the restaurant's busiest entrance.

definition: get or bring something back
memoryTip: Re-trieve: bring it back (like a retriever dog).
correctPassage: Archivists worked for hours to retrieve the damaged negatives from the flooded basement.
wrongPassages: She hoped to retrieve the lost email by drafting an entirely new message from scratch.
They tried to retrieve the meeting by canceling it before anyone could arrive.
He will retrieve the broken vase by leaving the shards scattered across the floor.

definition: make look or feel younger, fresher, or more vital
memoryTip: Re-juvenile: make young or fresh again.
correctPassage: A carefully planned renovation helped rejuvenate the aging civic center without erasing its original character.
wrongPassages: Long hours and skipped meals will rejuvenate students already worn down by exam season.
Dumping industrial runoff into the estuary is expected to rejuvenate the damaged fish populations.
The committee hoped to rejuvenate public trust by canceling services and raising fees across the board.

definition: difficult to understand
memoryTip: Abstract + obtuse difficulty — hard for most people to grasp.
correctPassage: Even specialists found the paper’s mathematical argument unusually abstruse.
wrongPassages: The abstruse safety poster used plain icons and one-line instructions anyone could follow.
Her abstruse overview summarized the main findings in three clear bullet points.
Students praised the textbook as abstruse because every concept came with a simple worked example.

definition: aggressive and ready to fight
memoryTip: Belli = war — speech or manner that is eager to fight.
correctPassage: Bellicose statements from both sides made a negotiated ceasefire increasingly unlikely.
wrongPassages: Her bellicose reply thanked the critics and invited them to a joint workshop.
The bellicose charter banned arms sales and established a permanent mediation board.
After the final, he offered a bellicose handshake and complimented the opposing coach.

definition: a harsh, jarring mixture of sounds
memoryTip: Caco (bad) + phony (sound) — a harsh clash of noise.
correctPassage: A cacophony of horns and sirens rose from the intersection after the power failed.
wrongPassages: Critics praised the ensemble’s cacophony for its seamless blend and soft dynamics.
The library’s cacophony rule allowed only whispered conversation in the reading rooms.
Listeners described the recording as pure cacophony, meaning each note sat perfectly in tune.

definition: causing harm or damage
memoryTip: Delete-erious: deletes health — harmful in effect.
correctPassage: Researchers warned that prolonged exposure to the solvent may have deleterious effects on memory.
wrongPassages: The physician called the treatment deleterious because patients recovered faster with almost no side effects.
Regular sleep and outdoor exercise had a deleterious impact on her stamina after the illness.
Officials praised the new guardrails for their deleterious influence on the number of serious crashes.

definition: showing rude or arrogant lack of respect
memoryTip: In-solent: so rude you feel the insult — cheeky disrespect.
correctPassage: The committee chair cut off the witness for an insolent remark that mocked the panel’s authority.
wrongPassages: Her insolent reply thanked the judges and deferred to every point they raised.
Staff described his insolent manner as careful, deferential, and free of sarcasm.
The manual praised insolent customer service that treated every complaint with patience and respect.

definition: the process of spreading more widely
memoryTip: Diffuse = scatter: ideas or particles spreading out.
correctPassage: Historians trace the diffusion of printing technology from a few workshops to presses across the continent.
wrongPassages: Strict export bans ensured the diffusion of the formula stayed locked inside a single laboratory.
The diffusion of the protest into one sealed auditorium kept the message from reaching the city.
Curators celebrated the sculpture’s diffusion by burying it in a private vault for decades.

definition: spoken or done without preparation
memoryTip: Ex tempore = out of the moment — no notes, no rehearsal.
correctPassage: When the projector failed, she offered an extemporaneous summary that still answered every key question.
wrongPassages: His extemporaneous lecture followed a script he had memorized over three full weeks.
The team filed an extemporaneous brief only after months of drafting and legal review.
An extemporaneous ceremony unfolded exactly as the printed program prescribed, line by line.

definition: tending to remind one of something
memoryTip: Reminisce = remember: reminiscent things spark old memories.
correctPassage: The café’s tiled floor was reminiscent of the station waiting room she had known as a child.
wrongPassages: Critics called the brand-new design reminiscent of nothing anyone could associate with prior work.
He stayed carefully reminiscent so that no detail of the past would ever come to mind.
A completely blank memory made the faded photograph feel intensely reminiscent of her childhood.

definition: deep-seated hostility or active opposition
memoryTip: Enemy + -ity: the state of being someone's enemy.
correctPassage: Decades of enmity between the two parties made even a brief joint appearance unlikely.
wrongPassages: Their lifelong enmity explained why they still mentored each other’s students without hesitation.
The club’s enmity toward newcomers was clear in the warm dinners held for every new member.
She felt only enmity for the colleague who had defended her work through every setback.

definition: abundant in quantity or supply
memoryTip: Copy lots: copious means there's plenty to go around.
correctPassage: The archival team catalogued copious correspondence between the ambassadors, filling several bound volumes.
wrongPassages: After successive droughts, the reservoir retained only a copious trickle of water.
Her copious remarks consisted of a single, carefully chosen sentence.
The museum's copious collection of Roman coins numbered fewer than a dozen pieces.

definition: find a way around an obstacle or rule
memoryTip: Circum- (around) + vent (go): slip around the barrier.
correctPassage: By filing under a different statute, the firm sought to circumvent the expired licensing requirement.
wrongPassages: The hikers circumvented the blocked trail by continuing straight along the same marked path.
Rather than avoid the ban, the company circumvented the regulation by complying with every clause.
She circumvented the difficult conversation by addressing the conflict directly and in full.

definition: make free from bacteria or other living microorganisms
memoryTip: Make sterile: kill germs so nothing can grow.
correctPassage: Before surgery, nurses sterilize the instruments in an autoclave to eliminate microbial contamination.
wrongPassages: Farmers sterilize the soil each spring by adding compost that encourages microbial growth.
The chef sterilized the cutting board by leaving it unwashed overnight on the counter.
Conservationists sterilize the wetland by introducing a greater diversity of plant and animal species.

definition: regularly found among a people or in a particular place
memoryTip: En-demos: native to a people/place, not a one-time visitor.
correctPassage: The rare orchid is endemic to the cloud forests of that range and is seldom found elsewhere.
wrongPassages: The illness was endemic for a single afternoon before vanishing from the region entirely.
Snow is endemic in the coastal desert, where it has been recorded only once in history.
An endemic visitor arrived from overseas for a brief conference and departed the next week.

definition: only slightly related to the main matter; diverging
memoryTip: Off on a tangent: barely touching the main point.
correctPassage: The committee set aside several tangential objections that did not bear on the proposal's central provisions.
wrongPassages: Her tangential analysis formed the core of the argument and resolved every outstanding dispute.
The tangential section of the report was devoted entirely to the study's primary research question.
Reviewers called the plan tangential because it addressed the core problem with precision.

definition: a stock of skills, pieces, or roles one can perform
memoryTip: Your repertory of tricks: the set of things you can do.
correctPassage: The pianist expanded her repertoire to include modern jazz standards.
wrongPassages: After abandoning every piece she could play, she claimed a richer repertoire than before.
The committee treated his single unrehearsed remark as the full repertoire of his expertise.
Clearing the stage between numbers steadily enlarged the orchestra's repertoire for the season.

definition: extend out beyond a surface or line
memoryTip: Jut out like a jaw: stick out past the edge.
correctPassage: Balconies jut over the street, shading the sidewalk below.
wrongPassages: The polished wall seemed to jut flush with the floor, offering no protrusion at all.
Crews jutted the fabric tight against the frame so that no edge extended outward.
The lake bed jutted deep underground, leaving no shoreline or outcrop above.

definition: relating to earthquakes; of enormous or sudden impact
memoryTip: Seismograph quake energy: huge shakes, literal or figurative.
correctPassage: The merger sent a seismic shock through the entire industry.
wrongPassages: The seismic revision was so minor that analysts dismissed it as routine noise.
Colleagues labeled her uneventful lunch break the most seismic hour of the workday.
A seismic hush barely registered in the archive, leaving the room undisturbed.

definition: a difficult, unpleasant, or embarrassing situation
memoryTip: Stuck in a pickle: a predicament is a hard spot to escape.
correctPassage: Without a spare tire, they faced a real predicament on the remote road.
wrongPassages: After years of careful saving, their predicament was a fully funded retirement.
Her predicament was so trivial that she resolved it in under a minute without help.
They celebrated the predicament of a flawlessly planned and uneventful expedition.

definition: responsibility for a fault or wrong; blameworthiness
memoryTip: Culpa = blame: culpability is how much fault you carry.
correctPassage: The inquiry assessed each manager's culpability for the safety failure.
wrongPassages: Proof of his complete innocence only strengthened claims of his culpability.
The foundation conferred culpability honors on volunteers who had committed no fault.
She accepted full culpability for a success that involved no error on her part.

definition: the act of distributing or spreading over a wide area
memoryTip: Disperse = scatter: dispersion is the spread itself.
correctPassage: Researchers tracked the dispersion of pollen across several neighboring valleys.
wrongPassages: The committee's dispersion of funds into a single account concentrated every grant.
Careful dispersion kept the rare manuscripts locked in one climate-controlled vault.
Her dispersion of the rumor meant she never repeated it outside the room.

definition: dig out earth and uncover by digging
memoryTip: Ex-cavate: dig out a cavity in the ground.
correctPassage: Archaeologists will excavate the burial site before the road construction begins.
wrongPassages: Crews excavate the trench each morning by refilling it with compacted soil.
She excavated the empty shelves by stacking additional cartons on top.
Engineers excavate the bridge deck when they pave a new surface over it.

definition: adorn with chains of flowers, lights, or fabric hung in loops
memoryTip: Festival loops: hang decorations in draping curves.
correctPassage: Staff festoon the courtyard with strings of lights for the evening reception.
wrongPassages: They festoon the ballroom by removing every banner and hanging ornament.
She festooned the report by underlining each heading in dense black ink.
Workers festoon the plaza when they polish the stone until it gleams.

definition: ordinary written or spoken language, as opposed to poetry
memoryTip: Not verse: prose is everyday sentences, not meter and rhyme.
correctPassage: The historian's prose is plain and direct, favoring short declarative sentences.
wrongPassages: Her latest prose depends on strict meter and end rhyme in every stanza.
He performed an improvised prose on the violin during the intermission.
Their prose arrangement for choir required four-part vocal harmony.

definition: angry or bitter conflict; struggle
memoryTip: Strive into conflict: strife is fighting and discord.
correctPassage: Years of regional strife disrupted trade along the mountain routes.
wrongPassages: Prolonged strife among the partners produced an unusually stable alliance.
The strife of the quiet library made it ideal for uninterrupted study.
They valued the strife of a household where no one ever argued.

definition: a cleverly devised plan, scheme, or device, often artificial
