memoryTip: Con-TRIVE-ance: a clever TRICK or device someone contrived.
correctPassage: Critics dismissed the subplot as a contrivance meant only to force the rivals into a final confrontation.
wrongPassages: Historians praised the treaty as a contrivance that arose without planning or human design.
The archaeologist labeled each fossil a contrivance because it had formed over millions of years.
After years of drought, the reservoir’s low level was a natural contrivance no engineer had engineered.

definition: to share a boundary with; touch along an edge
memoryTip: A-BUTT against: properties that butt up against each other.
correctPassage: The new library will abut the historic courthouse, sharing a continuous stone wall along the east side.
wrongPassages: The committee voted to abut the hearing until next month so members could review the report.
Her abrupt manners seemed to abut the guests, who left the dinner early.
Investors hoped the forecast would abut, offering precise figures for every quarter.

definition: persisting tirelessly; incapable of being worn out
memoryTip: In-de-FATIGUE-able: fatigue cannot stop you.
correctPassage: An indefatigable researcher returned to the archives each morning until the missing letters surfaced.
wrongPassages: After one short shift, the indefatigable intern asked to go home and sleep for the rest of the week.
The curator asked staff to indefatigable the exhibit cases before opening the gallery.
Surveyors recorded the bridge’s indefatigable as a span of nearly two hundred meters.

definition: written or published under a false name
memoryTip: PSEUDO + name: a fake name on the byline.
correctPassage: The essayist published a pseudonymous critique of the firm where she still worked under her real name.
wrongPassages: Once the orchestra drowned the choir, the voices sounded almost pseudonymous from the back row.
She submitted a pseudonymous application that listed only her legal name and government ID number.
The mayor hoped a live press conference would make the scandal pseudonymous by putting every detail on record.

definition: to gently push; to lightly encourage toward an action
memoryTip: Elbow NUDGE: a light push that steers without force.
correctPassage: A well-timed reminder can nudge employees to complete the survey before the deadline.
wrongPassages: The demolition crew gave the support beam one final nudge, and the entire structure collapsed.
A single nudge of the thrusters was enough to hurl the rocket beyond Earth’s atmosphere.
By late afternoon the harbor looked nudge, with tourist boats filling every available slip.

definition: to voluntarily give up or stop claiming something
memoryTip: Re-LINQUISH: let go of a claim or hold (think relinquish the crown).
correctPassage: After the merger, the founder agreed to relinquish day-to-day control of the company.
wrongPassages: Investors hoped to relinquish a larger share of the market through aggressive pricing.
She relinquished the scholarship by studying harder and raising her average.
The brief was so relinquish that jurors needed almost no further testimony.

definition: to confirm or support as true; to give a personal guarantee
memoryTip: VOUCH for a friend: put your word behind their honesty.
correctPassage: Two former supervisors will vouch for his reliability on the job.
wrongPassages: Several experts plan to vouch the methodology as too flawed for publication.
The editor tried to vouch the controversial findings by cutting the final section.
Analysts worked to vouch public opinion through a lengthy nationwide survey.

definition: providing additional help; serving as a secondary support
memoryTip: AUX jack: the extra, secondary connection that helps out.
correctPassage: The hospital kept an auxiliary power system ready in case the main grid failed.
wrongPassages: The auxiliary engine alone powered the entire vessel; no other motors were installed.
Please auxiliary the fragile samples before shipping them overseas.
Critics called the initiative auxiliary and therefore the project's sole priority.

definition: to lead an attack, campaign, or major effort
memoryTip: Tip of the SPEAR: you go first and lead the charge.
correctPassage: A small committee will spearhead fundraising for the new library wing.
wrongPassages: He agreed to spearhead the initiative only after every other department had finished its work.
Lobbyists worked to spearhead the reform bill by filing endless procedural delays.
Reviewers found the conclusion spearhead and unsupported by any of the data.

definition: to draw out a response, fact, or reaction
memoryTip: E-LICIT draws it out—don't confuse with illicit (illegal).
correctPassage: The interviewer's silence helped elicit a more candid answer from the witness.
wrongPassages: City council voted to elicit overnight parking near the transit station.
Officials rewrote the policy to elicit dissent before it could reach the press.
Alumni were asked to elicit funds for the new scholarship endowment.

definition: to assess the value, quality, or worth of something
memoryTip: APPRAise the price—assess value (not the same as praise).
correctPassage: Before listing the estate, the auction house hired a specialist to appraise the collection of rare maps.
wrongPassages: The audience stood to appraise the conductor after the final chord.
Editors agreed to appraise the manuscript by printing it without review.
She hoped the committee would appraise her proposal with a standing ovation.

definition: to perceive, detect, or recognize with care
memoryTip: DIS-cern: sift carefully until you can tell things apart.
correctPassage: From the blurred satellite image, analysts could still discern the outline of the abandoned runway.
wrongPassages: The firm decided to discern the outdated files by shredding them overnight.
They billed discern as a separate line item on every client invoice.
The supervisor asked staff to discern open tickets by auto-closing anything older than a week.

definition: clearly visible; attracting notice
memoryTip: Con-SPIC-uous: easy to SEE (Latin spicere) because it stands out.
correctPassage: The senator’s bright red scarf made her conspicuous among the gray coats on the steps.
wrongPassages: She kept the signed originals conspicuous in a locked vault no one ever opened.
Once the brass section covered the theme completely, the motif became especially conspicuous.
His muted, camouflaged jacket was chosen to be as conspicuous as possible in the forest.

definition: to formally declare that one is giving something up
memoryTip: Re-NOUNCE: publicly announce you are giving it up.
correctPassage: After the scandal, the heir chose to renounce any claim to the family title.
wrongPassages: Reviewers called the revised statistics renounce once the reanalysis confirmed the findings.
He planned to renounce the award by accepting it on live television.
The empty warehouse looked renounce after decades without tenants or cargo.

definition: a minor weakness or harmless eccentricity
memoryTip: A little FOIBLE is a foil-able flaw—minor, not fatal.
correctPassage: Colleagues forgave his only foible: rearranging every whiteboard marker by color before a meeting.
wrongPassages: Engineers traced the bridge collapse to a single foible in the main support beam.
Investors credited her foible leadership with rescuing the firm during the crisis.
The only foible in the reactor design was the complete absence of a cooling system.

definition: to express disapproval or disappointment; blame
memoryTip: Re-PROACH: approach someone again—with blame, not praise.
correctPassage: There was quiet reproach in the way she asked why he had missed the deadline.
wrongPassages: After the championship win, the coach offered only reproach, listing each player's strengths in detail.
Her letter of reproach thanked him warmly for every favor he had done.
The board's formal reproach endorsed the policy and recommended a raise for the director.

definition: showing scorn or deep disrespect
memoryTip: Full of CONTEMPT—scornful, looking down on someone.
correctPassage: His contemptuous shrug made it clear he thought the proposal was foolish.
wrongPassages: She gave a contemptuous smile that radiated pure admiration for the speaker.
In a contemptuous show of respect, he stood and applauded the critic's argument.
The mentor's contemptuous comments on the draft were full of encouragement and praise.

definition: very surprising or astonishing
memoryTip: Makes you START (jump)—so surprising you flinch.
correctPassage: The most startling finding was that sleep alone cut the error rate in half.
wrongPassages: Historians called the long-predicted election result startling, since polls had forecast it for months.
The lab reported a startling pattern: every trial matched the control with no unexpected deviation.
Her startling presentation simply repeated the three bullet points the team already knew by heart.

definition: to fail to give a true impression of; to contradict
memoryTip: Be-LIE: the surface lies about what is really underneath.
correctPassage: His calm tone belied how nervous he felt before the exam.
wrongPassages: Rising enrollment numbers belied the claim that the program was thriving.
Her tearful apology belied how sincerely sorry she felt after the mistake.
The detailed footnotes belied every source she cited, confirming each quotation line by line.

definition: peculiar to an individual; highly distinctive
memoryTip: IDIO + quirks: your personal odd habits and style.
correctPassage: Her idiosyncratic color code made the spreadsheet unreadable to anyone else on the team.
wrongPassages: Everyone followed the same idiosyncratic checklist issued by headquarters.
The style guide enforced one idiosyncratic format so that all reports looked identical.
Regulators praised the idiosyncratic protocol for eliminating personal variation across every lab.

definition: persistently demanding to the point of annoyance
memoryTip: Im-PORTUNE: keep porting the same ask until it’s annoying.
correctPassage: Importunate callers continued to press the office for an earlier hearing long after the deadline had passed.
wrongPassages: The importunate intern waited quietly and never repeated a request once it had been declined.
A single courteous note was enough to make her approach seem importunate to the entire board.
His importunate withdrawal from the debate left colleagues free of any further appeals.

definition: skill in performing tasks, especially with the hands
memoryTip: Dexterous hands — think “Dexter” building gadgets with skill.
correctPassage: Assembling the microcircuit demanded exceptional manual dexterity and steady focus.
wrongPassages: Judges praised his dexterity after he fumbled the tools and broke two samples.
The technician’s dexterity showed most clearly in how slowly and awkwardly she handled the instruments.
They measured the surgeon’s dexterity by how often instruments slipped from her grip.

definition: without regard to; regardless of
memoryTip: Ir-respective: without respect to X — regardless of it.
correctPassage: The scholarship is awarded on academic merit, irrespective of family income.
wrongPassages: Funding decisions were made irrespective of need, meaning only the wealthiest applicants were considered.
The policy applies irrespective of major only when the major is engineering.
She chose the laboratory assignment irrespective of her interest, carefully matching every preference.

definition: excessive pride in appearance or achievements
memoryTip: Vain about looks or status — vanity is that excessive pride.
correctPassage: Critics argued that the renovation was motivated more by vanity than by any genuine public need.
wrongPassages: Her vanity showed when she credited the whole team and stepped out of the commemorative photo.
He treated vanity as pure selflessness, quietly declining every award offered to him.
The plain cabin, built without mirrors or display, was widely admired as a monument to vanity.

definition: not transparent; hard to understand
memoryTip: Can’t see through it — glass that blocks light, or prose that blocks meaning.
correctPassage: The selection process remained opaque to anyone outside the small review committee.
wrongPassages: The glass partition was so opaque that every desk in the office was clearly visible from the hall.
Her opaque summary listed each step in plain language a newcomer could follow at once.
Editors praised the report as opaque because its logic was open and easy to check.

definition: many and of various types
memoryTip: Multi + farious forms — many varied kinds at once.
correctPassage: The archive's multifarious holdings span field notes, oral histories, and rare botanical sketches.
wrongPassages: Reviewers praised the report's multifarious focus on a single, narrowly defined case study.
The committee sought a multifarious policy that treated every district by the exact same rule.
Her multifarious wardrobe consisted of one navy blazer worn to every formal event.

definition: arranged in layers; divided into status levels
memoryTip: In strata (layers) — stacked rock or stacked social ranks.
correctPassage: Access to specialized care remained stratified by income, region, and insurance status.
wrongPassages: Geologists described the cliff as stratified after finding a single uniform deposit with no distinct bands.
They mixed the pigment until it was stratified into one smooth, undifferentiated color.
The firm insisted its workforce was stratified because every employee earned the same wage and title.

definition: having real importance or a firm basis
memoryTip: Has substance — real weight and importance, not fluff.
correctPassage: The board demanded substantive revisions to the budget, not cosmetic wording changes.
wrongPassages: They called the plan substantive even though it offered only vague slogans and no data.
They labeled the empty press release substantive for using elegant stationery and a formal seal.
A substantive edit left every flawed claim intact while adding several pages of filler.

definition: a long step; progress made
memoryTip: A long step forward — or progress (“made great strides”).
correctPassage: Public health agencies made a significant stride in reducing childhood infection rates.
wrongPassages: After months of setbacks, the team celebrated a stride that returned them to the project's starting point.
Her stride across the stage was a sequence of tiny, hesitant shuffles between the microphones.
Missing every milestone was treated as a stride toward completing the product on schedule.

definition: proceeding gradually and subtly with harmful effects
memoryTip: In-side-ious: harm sneaks in from inside before you notice.
correctPassage: An insidious form of measurement bias can quietly distort results long before anyone notices.
wrongPassages: The hazard was insidious: alarms sounded and warning signs marked every entrance in bright red.
Colleagues trusted his insidious candor, which left motives open and tricks impossible.
They welcomed the insidious reform that openly corrected every flaw in a single afternoon.

definition: bring oneself into favor through flattery or effort to please
memoryTip: In + graces: flattery to get into someone’s good graces.
correctPassage: Hoping for a promotion, the junior analyst tried to ingratiate herself with the partners by taking on thankless assignments.
wrongPassages: His decision to challenge the chair’s proposal in open session was an attempt to ingratiate himself with the committee.
She managed to ingratiate the rival department by blocking every request for shared resources.
The envoy sought to ingratiate the host government by publicly dismissing its concerns.

definition: excessively talkative, especially about trivial matters
memoryTip: A garrulous guest pours a garbled river of endless small talk.
correctPassage: A garrulous seatmate turned the short flight into an unbroken stream of minor anecdotes.
wrongPassages: Editors preferred the garrulous brief because it cut every unnecessary detail.
The garrulous archivist rarely spoke and answered questions only in writing.
Colleagues valued her garrulous manner for how quickly she moved past small talk.

definition: intensely enthusiastic or passionate
memoryTip: Fervor on fire — fervid means passion running hot.
correctPassage: Fervid supporters of the reform filled the hearing room hours before the session began.
wrongPassages: His fervid reaction to the announcement was a shrug and a request to adjourn.
Critics called the novel fervid for its cool detachment and carefully understated tone.
The committee’s fervid endorsement consisted of polite silence and no further comment.

definition: pressing; demanding immediate attention
memoryTip: Exigent = emergency-urgent — it demands attention now.
correctPassage: Auditors described the funding shortfall as exigent, prompting the board to meet that evening.
wrongPassages: Because the request was exigent, staff were told they could respond whenever convenient.
He filed the exigent forms several months late with no sense of urgency.
The optional survey was labeled exigent so employees would feel free to ignore it.

definition: understood by only a small specialist group
memoryTip: Eso-teric: for the inner circle only — specialist knowledge.
correctPassage: The paper’s esoteric methodology limited its readership to specialists in the field.
wrongPassages: The esoteric handbook became required reading in nearly every introductory course.
She favored esoteric explanations because they used only everyday vocabulary.
Networks chose esoteric programming precisely for its broad popular appeal.

definition: drain of energy; weaken
memoryTip: E-nerve-ate: strip the nerve/energy out — weaken (not energize!).
correctPassage: Weeks of intense heat and little shade began to enervate the research crew.
wrongPassages: A short rest and a cold drink will enervate the runners before the final mile.
The coach hoped a fiery speech would enervate the team for a stronger second half.
Proper sleep and nutrition enervate athletes, restoring strength after hard training.

definition: hostile and aggressive
memoryTip: Belli- (war) + gerent — warlike and ready to fight.
correctPassage: The ambassador's belligerent reply made further compromise seem unlikely.
wrongPassages: Her belligerent manner—patient questions and careful listening—calmed the room.
The panel praised his belligerent diplomacy for defusing disputes before they grew.
A belligerent host offered tea and soft music to put every guest at ease.

definition: wanting or devouring great quantities of something
memoryTip: Vora = devour — a huge appetite for food, books, or work.
correctPassage: A voracious reader, she finished several dense histories each month.
wrongPassages: His voracious lunch left him satisfied after only a few crackers and water.
The board's voracious agenda left long empty afternoons with little left to review.
She was a voracious student who rarely completed more than a page of any assignment.

definition: a change of circumstances, often unwelcome
memoryTip: Vici-change: the ups and downs fortune throws at you.
correctPassage: The firm survived every vicissitude of the volatile market cycle.
wrongPassages: Life under the stable regime was one long vicissitude of unbroken calm.
They planned for vicissitude by freezing every policy for the next decade.
The lake's remarkable vicissitude kept its waterline fixed year after year.

definition: looking or sounding sad and dismal
memoryTip: Lugubrious funeral face — exaggeratedly mournful and gloomy.
correctPassage: A lugubrious score made the short documentary feel heavier than its runtime.
wrongPassages: His lugubrious welcome—a bright grin and an easy joke—lifted the mood at once.
The festival stayed lugubrious with brass bands, confetti, and dancing crowds.
She delivered a lugubrious toast that left the guests laughing for several minutes.

definition: subject to sudden or unpredictable mood changes
memoryTip: Mercury races across the sky—mercurial people change moods just as fast.
correctPassage: Colleagues found his mercurial temperament hard to anticipate from one meeting to the next.
wrongPassages: The treaty rested on mercurial commitments that never shifted over decades of enforcement.
She kept a mercurial routine that began at the same hour and followed the same steps every day.
Investors preferred mercurial leadership that held a single strategy through every market swing.

definition: excessively obedient or attentive; servile
memoryTip: Obey-sequious: so eager to please it turns into fawning.
correctPassage: Obsequious aides rushed to fulfill every minor request before it was fully spoken.
wrongPassages: His obsequious defiance of the chair’s instructions delayed the entire session.
The reviewer’s obsequious critique dismantled the author’s central claims without apology.
She was so obsequious that she declined every invitation from senior faculty and kept her distance.

definition: done secretly, especially because it would not be approved
memoryTip: Surreptitious sneak—on the sly because it wouldn't be allowed.
correctPassage: A surreptitious transfer of files during the audit later triggered a formal investigation.
wrongPassages: The governor’s surreptitious speech was broadcast live to every household in the state.
Their surreptitious petition hung in the lobby with a sign-up sheet open to all visitors.
She posted a surreptitious memo on the shared drive and emailed the whole staff a link.

definition: having knowledge of events before they take place
memoryTip: Pre-science: knows what will happen before it does.
correctPassage: Her prescient essay on supply-chain fragility was widely cited after the shortages arrived.
wrongPassages: His prescient brief merely restated yesterday’s headlines without anticipating further risk.
The prescient study refused to offer any forecast and limited itself to past measurements.
Editors called the timeline prescient because it recorded each development only after it occurred.

definition: attacking or rejecting cherished beliefs or institutions
memoryTip: Icon-clast: smashes sacred icons—challenges tradition.
correctPassage: An iconoclastic monograph questioned long-standing assumptions about the discipline’s founding figures.
wrongPassages: The museum’s iconoclastic catalog reproduced every traditional attribution without challenge.
Her iconoclastic devotion to the original bylaws left no room for reform of any kind.
Directors praised his iconoclastic habit of defending each inherited policy against revision.

definition: in a brief and clearly expressed manner
memoryTip: Succinct = cinched tight like a belt—short and clear.
correctPassage: The researcher summarized her findings succinctly, distilling months of data into a few precise claims.
wrongPassages: He described the proposal so succinctly that the presentation stretched well past the allotted hour.
The memo was written succinctly, wandering through several digressions before reaching its point.
She answered the question succinctly by repeating the same anecdote with ever more detail.

definition: showing great attention to correct detail or form
memoryTip: Punctual about points—picky about every detail of etiquette.
correctPassage: A punctilious archivist corrected every citation so that no source was incomplete or mislabeled.
wrongPassages: His punctilious review of the application skipped the required forms and ignored the dress code.
She was too punctilious to notice that the contract bore the wrong date and signature.
The punctilious clerk filed every document into a single unmarked drawer without sorting them.

definition: weird, sinister, or ghostly
memoryTip: Elder-witch eerie—uncanny, weird, and ghostly.
correctPassage: An eldritch light over the marsh made the abandoned mill seem less abandoned than watching.
wrongPassages: The eldritch kitchen felt warm and ordinary after a long day of errands.
Neighbors described the eldritch block party as cheerful, familiar, and entirely predictable.
She preferred eldritch lighting that left every corner of the room bright and inviting.

definition: make obscure or unintelligible
memoryTip: Ob-fus-cate: cloud over—deliberately make it hard to understand.
correctPassage: Dense legal jargon can obfuscate responsibility rather than make it plain to the public.
wrongPassages: The diagram was redesigned to obfuscate the process so beginners could follow each step.
Teachers asked students to obfuscate their main claim in one clear, direct sentence.
The FAQ was rewritten to obfuscate common questions with plain-language answers.

definition: express fluently and coherently
memoryTip: Clear joints of speech—express ideas smoothly and clearly.
correctPassage: Few candidates could articulate a coherent plan for reforming the district's budget.
wrongPassages: He could only articulate in broken fragments that left the audience more confused than before.
She refused to articulate any position, remaining silent through the entire debate.
His attempt to articulate dissolved into mumbled half-sentences no one could parse.

definition: the highest point; ideal or culminating example
memoryTip: Apo-theos: raised to godlike status—the peak or ideal.
correctPassage: Critics hailed the final movement as the apotheosis of the composer's lifelong work with form.
wrongPassages: The committee treated the unfinished draft as the apotheosis of a project still lacking direction.
After years of decline, the firm reached its apotheosis when sales hit their lowest recorded level.
Historians dated the apotheosis of the movement to the decade before it had any public influence.

definition: describing a work of visual art in literary form
memoryTip: Ekphrasis = words that re-paint art—a poem about a painting.
correctPassage: Her ekphrastic sequence answers the museum triptych stanza by stanza in carefully paced prose.
wrongPassages: The biologist's ekphrastic chart tracked enzyme rates without describing any painting or sculpture.
Reviewers called the purely fiscal brief ekphrastic even though it never engaged a work of visual art.
He delivered an ekphrastic inventory of warehouse stock, item by item, with no artistic subject.

definition: relating to an agent or the capacity to act
memoryTip: Agent-ial: about who can act—having agency.
correctPassage: The study emphasizes the agential role of local organizers in shaping the reform.
wrongPassages: Observers called the policy agential precisely because citizens had no room to choose or resist.
Critics found the protagonist agential only in the chapters where outside forces decided every outcome.
The dormant machinery was labeled agential while it remained powered down and untouched for months.

definition: the state of being annoyed or worried
memoryTip: Vexed feeling—annoyance, irritation, fret.
correctPassage: Repeated schedule changes became a steady source of vexation for the research team.
wrongPassages: The quiet afternoon brought a rare vexation of ease that settled over the entire household.
She recalled the promotion with pure vexation, smiling at how perfectly everything had aligned.
The reunion filled him with vexation so complete he could not stop laughing in relief.

definition: words that imitate the sound they name
memoryTip: Buzz, hiss, boom—words that sound like what they mean.
correctPassage: In the graphic novel, each collision panel is edged with bold onomatopoeia that echoes the impact.
wrongPassages: The silent geometry treatise was praised for its onomatopoeia, though no word mimicked a sound.
She classified abstract ledger terms such as equity and liability as onomatopoeia.
His onomatopoeia chapter surveyed only color gradients and never a sound-imitating word.

definition: not honorable in character or purpose
memoryTip: Ig-noble: not noble—base or dishonorable motives.
correctPassage: Historians condemned the minister's ignoble decision to sacrifice allied troops for a short-term political gain.
wrongPassages: The firefighter's ignoble rescue of trapped residents was cited as a model of civic courage.
Donors praised the foundation's ignoble campaign to expand scholarships in rural schools.
Her ignoble career of public service earned tributes from rivals as well as supporters.

definition: steal
memoryTip: Purloin = quietly pocket something that isn't yours.
correctPassage: A clerk had managed to purloin several confidential files from the locked records room overnight.
wrongPassages: She offered to purloin the manuscript by delivering it safely to the publisher the next morning.
The museum planned to purloin the artifact by restoring it and returning it to the heirs.
He promised to purloin the borrowed equipment by placing it back on the workshop shelves.

definition: bold and without shame
memoryTip: Brass-bold—shamelessly bold, like polished brass.
correctPassage: In a brazen challenge to the rules, the lobbyist announced the deal before negotiations had closed.
wrongPassages: His brazen apology was whispered in private and heavy with visible remorse.
She made a brazen request only after carefully hiding her identity from every official.
The brazen witness avoided eye contact, stammered, and asked to leave the hearing.

definition: open to bribery; corruptible
memoryTip: Venal for sale—open to bribes and corruption.
correctPassage: Investigators exposed a venal inspector who approved unsafe sites in exchange for cash payments.
wrongPassages: The venal magistrate refused every gift and reported the offer to prosecutors.
Voters trusted his venal record of rejecting donations from industry lobbyists.
Her venal code of ethics barred staff from accepting favors of any kind.

definition: a surface reused after earlier writing was erased; layered history
memoryTip: Scraped parchment rewritten—old layers still show through.
correctPassage: Archaeologists called the plaza a palimpsest, each pavement laid over faint traces of an earlier one.
wrongPassages: He treated the brand-new blank notebook as a palimpsest, untouched by any prior writing.
Because the form could be filled out only once, the clerk labeled it a palimpsest.
The wall poured that morning, with no earlier design beneath it, was praised as a perfect palimpsest.

definition: a filmmaker whose personal style dominates their work
memoryTip: French “author” of film — the director’s signature is on every frame.
correctPassage: Critics praised the filmmaker as an auteur whose visual language was unmistakable across every project.
wrongPassages: The studio hired an auteur mainly to manage ticket sales and concession inventory.
Reviewers called the editor an auteur because she deferred entirely to the producer’s choices.
As an auteur, the director insisted on remaining anonymous so no personal style would mark the film.

definition: confuse; make muddy or unclear
memoryTip: Be + muddle — stir into mud so nothing is clear.
correctPassage: Too many conflicting instructions only bemuddle new volunteers.
wrongPassages: A single clarifying diagram will bemuddle the procedure for first-time users.
The historian tried to bemuddle the timeline by arranging events in strict chronological order.
Clear section headings are designed to bemuddle the argument rather than scatter it.

definition: fleeting; lasting only a short time
memoryTip: Related to flee/fugitive — it flees quickly; here and gone.
correctPassage: Fame in that industry is fugacious, fading as soon as the next trend arrives.
wrongPassages: The treaty established a fugacious alliance expected to endure for generations.
Geologists described the mountain range as fugacious because it had stood unchanged for millennia.
She sought a fugacious career path, one that would remain stable and predictable for decades.

definition: very typical of a certain kind; model of a type
memoryTip: Archetype = original mold — the classic, textbook example.
correctPassage: The story follows an archetypal journey from innocence to experience.
wrongPassages: Her approach was so archetypal that no earlier model or convention could describe it.
Critics called the design archetypal precisely because it broke every established pattern in the field.
Biologists labeled the specimen archetypal when it matched none of the known traits of its species.

definition: the most perfect or pure example of a quality
memoryTip: Fifth essence (perfect core) — the purest, most classic example.
correctPassage: The café is the quintessential neighborhood hangout: crowded, informal, and known to everyone on the block.
wrongPassages: The proposal was quintessential of the genre in that it shared almost none of its usual features.
Reviewers called the draft quintessential because it was a rough outline missing every key component.
A quintessential sample of the data set would be one that is incomplete, outlier-heavy, and unrepresentative.

definition: the state of lasting only a short time
memoryTip: Transient = temporary — the short-lived nature of a thing.
correctPassage: The essay reflects on the transience of childhood friendships that fade after a single school year.
wrongPassages: Builders chose granite for its transience, expecting the memorial to last for centuries.
Economists celebrated the economy’s transience, pointing to decades of uninterrupted growth.
The archivist valued the manuscript’s transience, confident that its ink would never fade.

definition: unfair bias; a particular liking
memoryTip: Partial to one side — a soft spot, or unfair favoritism.
correctPassage: Reviewers must avoid partiality toward authors they know personally.
wrongPassages: Her partiality as a mediator consisted of refusing to favor either side in the dispute.
Scientists aim for partiality so that personal preferences never color their conclusions.
Judges praised the ruling’s partiality for weighing both arguments with equal care.

definition: difficult to accept or find pleasant
memoryTip: Can’t palate it — hard to swallow, whether food or truth.
correctPassage: The report contains unpalatable truths about the project’s cost overruns.
wrongPassages: Voters found the tax plan so unpalatable that they approved it without debate.
Critics called the ending unpalatable and recommended the film to every friend.
The compromise proved unpalatable to both parties, who signed it eagerly that afternoon.

definition: produce and discharge a substance; or hide away
memoryTip: Secret-e: hide it away — or glands secrete fluids.
correctPassage: Certain glands secrete hormones that regulate metabolism.
wrongPassages: Editors hoped to secrete the scandal by printing it on the front page of every edition.
City planners hoped to secrete congestion by opening two additional bridges.
The studio planned to secrete the premiere date on billboards across the city.

definition: a condition that limits a statement; or a credential
memoryTip: A qualifying limit softens a claim — or a credential that certifies you.
correctPassage: She accepted the praise with one important qualification about the study’s small sample.
wrongPassages: The recipe called for two qualifications of oil, measured roughly by eye.
He praised the proposal without qualification, then spent an hour listing its serious flaws.
The referee issued a qualification that removed the player from the rest of the match.

definition: careful thought; or something given in exchange
memoryTip: Careful thought — or the thing given in a deal (legal sense).
correctPassage: After lengthy consideration of the budget forecasts, the board postponed expansion.
wrongPassages: She showed consideration for the neighbors by blasting music until well after midnight.
Their consideration of the proposal lasted three seconds before automatic approval.
The engineer measured consideration in milliliters before sealing the sample vial.

definition: marked by decline or luxurious self-indulgence
memoryTip: De-cadence: falling from standards — luxuriously self-indulgent decline.
correctPassage: Critics called the empire’s late art decadent, devoted more to luxury than to reform.
wrongPassages: The frugal meal was decadent: plain rice, water, and lights out by eight.
Her decadent training plan eliminated every indulgence and tracked sleep to the minute.
Historians praised the decade as decadent for its strict discipline and civic restraint.

definition: put at risk of harm
memoryTip: In peril — placed in danger.
correctPassage: Rising seas have imperiled several coastal archaeological sites.
wrongPassages: New flood barriers have imperiled downtown by shielding it from storm surges.
The lab imperiled the samples by storing them in redundant locked freezers.
Conservators imperiled the manuscript when they restored and catalogued every page.

definition: playfully dishonest or mischievous
memoryTip: Like a charming rogue — mischievous, not fully serious.
correctPassage: A roguish smile after the prank made it hard for anyone to stay angry.
wrongPassages: The auditor’s roguish report cited every source and avoided even mild exaggeration.
She gave a roguish apology that listed each offense and accepted full blame without humor.
Judges called the ruling roguish because it carefully weighed both sides without flourish.

definition: relating to a roguish hero’s episodic adventures
memoryTip: Picaro = rogue hero — a rascal’s string of misadventures.
correctPassage: The novel is picaresque: a clever outsider stumbles through one misadventure after another.
wrongPassages: The biography is picaresque in its single fixed setting and solemn, linear chronology.
Engineers filed a picaresque report that catalogued every stress test with no narrative detours.
Reviewers called the treatise picaresque for its rigid structure and absence of a wandering hero.

definition: change direction when passing through a medium
memoryTip: Re-fract light: bend it as it passes through glass or water.
correctPassage: Sunlight refracts as it enters the denser water, making the submerged oar appear bent.
wrongPassages: The committee agreed to refract the proposal until a later session.
Historians refract the archive by sorting every document into labeled folders.
She tried to refract her criticism so that no one would feel hurt by it.

definition: standard or commonly used; not original
memoryTip: Off-the-shelf stock answer — standard, not original.
correctPassage: The mayor offered a stock reply that could have applied to almost any civic dispute.
wrongPassages: Her stock analysis introduced a framework no prior study had considered.
Reviewers praised the stock plot for abandoning every familiar narrative pattern.
He delivered a stock argument so idiosyncratic that colleagues could not place it.

definition: a sudden invasion or raid into territory
memoryTip: In + course/run — a sudden run into someone else’s ground.
correctPassage: The brief border incursion forced neighboring states to reinforce their patrols.
wrongPassages: A long period of peaceful trade was described as a commercial incursion.
Scholars called the gradual cultural exchange over centuries a quiet incursion.
The treaty formalized an incursion of goodwill that ended all hostilities.

definition: give or enhance the value or status of
memoryTip: Valor + ize — assign value or raise the status of something.
correctPassage: Recent scholarship has sought to valorize oral histories once dismissed as unreliable.
wrongPassages: Critics moved to valorize the novel by arguing it had no literary merit.
The board tried to valorize the program by cutting its funding entirely.
Editors valorized the manuscript when they rejected it without comment.

definition: destroy a large proportion of
memoryTip: Originally kill every tenth; now destroy a large share.
correctPassage: A prolonged drought can decimate crop yields across an entire region.
wrongPassages: The new hiring plan will decimate the workforce by adding dozens of positions.
Steady rainfall decimated the orchard by restoring the trees to full health.
Conservators decimated the collection when they restored and catalogued every item.
